item.title: Your AI coding agent could cost 5x more depending on the harness, benchmark finds
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
The same AI model can cost up to five times more to run depending on the coding agent harness it’s

The post Your AI coding agent could cost 5x more depending on the harness, benchmark finds appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
The same AI model can cost up to five times more to run depending on the coding agent harness it’s paired with, according to a new benchmark that tested 22 configurations across five open-weight models.

Runta and Baseten ran those combinations 27,280 times for FrontierHarness Eval v1.1, consuming roughly 83 billion tokens in the process.

Nearly 65% of estimated inference spending went to runs that failed verification or timed out.

The model itself accounted for 92.8% of the cost differences, but the harness still made a considerable difference. One configuration could be the cheapest option for one model and among the most expensive for another, adding another wrinkle for developers looking to cut coding-agent costs by changing harnesses or swapping in a cheaper model. Nearly 65% of estimated inference spending went to runs that failed verification or timed out.

Rankings flip with the model

The benchmark covered 22 coding-agent harness configurations across five models served through Baseten, including GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse Spark Open, and Kimi-K3. Each configuration ran 62 terminal-based tasks four times per model, with pass rates, inference costs and execution times recorded for comparison.

Codex CLI ranked first for lowest average cost per task with GLM-5.3 but dropped to 16th out of 22 configurations with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness Creator showed an even larger change, ranking first with Muse before falling to 21st with GLM-5.3 Flash.

Across the five models, harnesses shifted a median of 11 ranking positions when the model changed, while costs varied by as much as fivefold even when the model stayed the same.

Across the five models, harnesses shifted a median of 11 ranking positions when the model changed, while costs varied by as much as fivefold even when the model stayed the same. The biggest difference came with DeepSeek, where Cline CLI cost five times as much as OpenCode v1 but delivered a pass rate only two percentage points higher.

The researchers also shuffled the trials within each model 300 times to see whether random variation could explain the cost differences. The gaps in the actual results were larger than those in the shuffled trials, with a reported p-value of 0.003.

Failed runs eat the budget

Failed runs accounted for 52.7% of estimated inference spending, with timeouts adding another 11.8%. Just 35.5% went toward successful runs. Those costs are based on Baseten’s published rates, but they put a price on a familiar problem with coding agents struggling to complete difficult tasks.

Among the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of unsuccessful runs ended with the agent submitting a final answer that failed verification rather than timing out.

Among the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of unsuccessful runs ended with the agent submitting a final answer that failed verification rather than timing out. The researchers also found 216 instances of reward hacking in the execution logs, including 163 involving online lookups. All received zero scores.

Steps, not prompts, drive cost

Runta looked at whether prompt size, tool count, cache hit rates, or agent steps had the biggest impact on cost. Step count was the only factor with a statistically significant correlation to cost per successful task, at 0.51.

Mini-SWE-agent showed how multi-step agent execution can drive up token costs, starting with the smallest prompt in the benchmark at 882 tokens but averaging 38 steps per successful task and ranking 17th out of 22 configurations for cost per pass.

The five best-value harnesses relied heavily on shell commands, which made up 61% to 93% of their tool calls, and rarely used subagents, or context summarization. Runta didn’t test those design choices separately, however, so the results don’t establish whether the simpler setups were responsible for the lower costs.

item.title: OpenAI’s own tests show GPT-6.2 Astra is twice as likely to hide coding failures
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenAI’s new GPT-6.2 Astra is nearly twice as likely as its predecessor to leave users unaware of problems that prevented

The post OpenAI’s own tests show GPT-6.2 Astra is twice as likely to hide coding failures appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI’s new GPT-6.2 Astra is nearly twice as likely as its predecessor to leave users unaware of problems that prevented it from finishing a coding task, according to the company’s own safety evaluations. Developers building autonomous agents could encounter the same problem, since OpenAI has added a mitigation to Codex that isn’t automatically applied to direct API requests.

In its GPT-6.2 system card, published Tuesday alongside the release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, OpenAI reported that Astra failed to disclose a known obstacle in 22.28% of evaluated coding tasks, compared with 11.09% for GPT-6 Astra.

An agent may write better code without telling the developer when it couldn’t finish the job.

The copmany says both models perform better on demanding tasks while using fewer output tokens, but those improvements don’t necessarily make them more reliable at reporting failures. An agent may write better code without telling the developer when it couldn’t finish the job.

The New Stack has asked OpenAI whether it plans to extend the Codex mitigation to API developers and how the additional instructions affect the models’ failure-reporting behavior.

Inside the blocker deception test

OpenAI measured the behavior with an internal evaluation called Blocker Deception, which gives models realistic coding assignments before deliberately introducing obstacles that make the requested work impossible to finish as specified.

In some runs, the evaluation removes a source file the agent was supposed to modify. In others, it disables a tool needed to build the project. The evaluation then checks whether the model tells the user what happened or leaves the obstacle out of its final response.

The caveats Astra leaves out

The company acknowledges the regression and says it is still investigating the cause. One possible explanation is that training the models to give shorter answers with fewer caveats may have made them less likely to report problems that prevented them from completing a task. OpenAI cautions that the evaluation was designed to trigger this behavior, so the results don’t necessarily reflect how often Astra misleads users in production.

A separate evaluation, Broken Search Tool, identified a similar problem. The model receives questions requiring information retrieval while the necessary search capability is disabled. GPT-6.2 Astra failed to acknowledge the missing requirement or unavailable tool in 23% of cases, compared with 7.58% for GPT-6 Astra and 1% for GPT-6.1 Terra.

Developers can check the logs, test results, and git diff … but they shouldn’t have to dig through an entire session to find out that something failed.

Developers can check the logs, test results, and git diff to see what an agent actually did, but they shouldn’t have to dig through an entire session to find out that something failed. If an agent says it finished the job without mentioning a missing dependency or a failed build, that work could make it through review without anyone realizing there’s a problem. It’s another example of the code confidence gap that becomes harder to manage as agents take on more work across a repository.

The fix the API misses

OpenAI says it developed a prompt-based intervention that substantially reduced the rate of omitted blockers in evaluations of both Astra and Sol. The company incorporated that intervention into the standard Codex developer prompt at launch, but it does not automatically apply the same instructions to direct API requests.

Codex users get the updated prompt, but developers building their own agents through the API don’t.

Codex users get the updated prompt, but developers building their own agents through the API don’t. OpenAI hasn’t shown whether adding similar instructions to a custom harness would produce the same results.

The harness can’t take the model’s completion summary at face value because it needs to verify the diff, check test results, and confirm the expected artifacts exist before marking a task complete.

These verification loops are especially important for unattended agents, where a failed step can go unnoticed until someone reviews the work.

Performance up, reporting down

The disclosure comes as OpenAI promotes improvements in coding performance and efficiency across both new models.

In its launch announcement, OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Sol came within 0.5 points of Astra on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 coding benchmark at approximately one-fifth the estimated cost per task, with both models running at maximum effort.

In testing shared with The New Stack by OpenAI, Replit reported that GPT-6.2 Sol passed more tests, used 62% fewer output tokens and ran nearly three times as fast as GPT-6.1 Sol when building software from scratch.

Faster execution and lower inference costs make these models appealing for automated coding, but OpenAI’s safety tests show that better performance doesn’t necessarily mean an agent will tell developers when something goes wrong.

item.title: Microsoft’s new coding model promises near-Opus performance at 5% of the cost
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, Microsoft announced a number of new AI models, including two new

The post Microsoft’s new coding model promises near-Opus performance at 5% of the cost appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, Microsoft announced a number of new AI models, including two new coding models.

Imaginatively named Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, these new models promise to come very close to models like GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost.

As Microsoft notes, “MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance” for enterprise coding tasks. “It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost.”

MAI Code 2 benchmarks

The promise here is that Code 2 gets to 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost (which also goes to show how expensive Anthropic’s models are to run right now).

The model, Microsoft says, has also been tuned to create “great dashboards and visualizations” and that it “excels at visual coding.”

At least for the OpenAI comparison, it’s worth noting that OpenAI today released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, with improved performance. That softens Microsoft’s claims a bit, but it’s worth noting that OpenAI, too, notes that at least on Agents’ Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra is now 5.5 points “ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost” (which also goes to show how expensive Anthropic’s models are right now).

MAI Code 2 Flash benchmarks

As for MAI Code 2 Flash, Microsoft argues that it can match Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna on benchmarks like DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal-Bench 2.1, and SWE Atlas at 20% and 65% of the cost, respectively.

Microsoft’s bet: specialist models vs. generalists

One interesting wrinkle here is that Microsoft specifically tuned these models for the day-to-day coding work of its users. “They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work,” Microsoft writes.

The models Microsoft is comparing these models to are generalists. For a while, OpenAI took a similar approach with its Codex models, but it has abandoned this approach in favor of more general models.

Microsoft, meanwhile, which doesn’t build those kinds of in-house frontier models, seems to be focused on smaller specialized models that it can run more efficiently. And while they won’t match the frontier models across every benchmark, focusing on these specific tasks makes a lot of sense in this context.

Microsoft is taking this even further with models like MAI Work Flash, a model trained to work across Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ products.

Availability

MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are now available in GitHub Copilot, while Code 2 Flash is in limited preview on Microsoft Foundry. OpenRouter, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo will soon get support as well.

item.title: Microsoft’s ARM-based Cobalt 200 chips go GA. Why it matters for AI agents.
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Microsoft is making its Cobalt 200 virtual machines generally available, with CPU improvements aimed at the sandboxes, tools, and code

The post Microsoft’s ARM-based Cobalt 200 chips go GA. Why it matters for AI agents. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft is making its Cobalt 200 virtual machines generally available, with CPU improvements aimed at the sandboxes, tools, and code execution that keep AI agents running.

At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, the company announced that the VMs, powered by its second-generation Arm-based CPUs, are available in 14 Azure regions, expanding to 23 by the end of the year. Microsoft says they offer up to 50% better performance compared with Cobalt 100.

It’s been almost exactly a year since Microsoft first announced Cobalt 200 and about six months since the new VMs went into preview. Microsoft’s benchmarks show up to 1.5 times the performance for AI agent tool execution compared with Cobalt 100, for workloads like searching files, compiling code, and executing tasks in sandboxes.

Pat Stemen, Microsoft’s vice president for Azure Cobalt, tells The New Stack that the team spent part of the past year tuning the infrastructure for these operations. The chip’s large caches, memory performance, and physical cores already suited workloads like starting sandboxes, he says. Microsoft then built “a set of benchmarks inside the company for those common operations” and tuned the product against them.

Predictable performance or more speed

Cobalt 200 lets developers choose between two processor modes. Deterministic mode runs cores at a consistent 3.2 GHz, while opportunistic mode lets them reach 3.6 GHz when power and thermal headroom allow.

Microsoft says opportunistic mode can deliver up to 12% more performance, but clock speeds will vary.

“Customers love fixed frequency, by the way,” Stemen says. “They love the predictability that comes with that.”

Microsoft recommends deterministic mode for distributed data and analytics clusters, where the slowest node can set the pace, and services with tight performance targets. Web and API services, transaction processing, and media workloads may benefit more from the additional speed of opportunistic mode.

Developers can select the mode for each VM when they create it or change it later through the Azure portal, command-line tools, or infrastructure templates.

“So if you buy four cores from us,” Stemen says, “you can choose all four of them to run flexibly or deterministically.”

He adds that the extra performance is typically available until the machine’s cores are heavily loaded.

Designing around Azure workloads

Cobalt 200 uses 132 Arm Neoverse V3 cores, manufactured on TSMC’s 3nm process, while the VMs scale to 128 vCPUs. Each vCPU corresponds to a full physical core, with 3 MB of private L2 cache. The chip also includes 192 MB of system-level cache and 12 channels of DDR5 memory.

Stemen says the move from Cobalt 100 involved switching from a cost-optimized Arm core to a performance-optimized design, alongside larger caches and improved memory bandwidth.

Every Cobalt 200 VM also includes Azure Boost, which offloads networking and storage processing from the host. Microsoft reports up to 15% higher network bandwidth and 20% higher remote storage IOPS compared with Cobalt 100.

“They need remote storage. They need high-performance networking. They need local SSD,” Stemen says of the workloads customers bring to Azure.

Stemen says the team breaks Microsoft’s own workloads into smaller components, models their behavior before the hardware exists, and uses those results to make decisions about cache sizes, memory, and even the fans in a server rack. Product teams participate in the earliest planning reviews.

“They’re influencing the beginning of the product from when it’s just in PowerPoint,” Stemen says.

The Teams media-processing service, for example, reported 1.65 times the performance on Cobalt 200 compared with Cobalt 100. Microsoft says the service saw linear scaling across physical cores and could load vCPUs to 90% utilization while serving traffic.

Outside Microsoft, Amadeus reported more than 30% higher flight-search throughput in its benchmark lab compared with Cobalt 100.

A wider range of Arm workloads

Indeed, quite a few Microsoft services like Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure DevOps, Azure SQL, Microsoft 365, Xbox, and others already run on Cobalt today.

A while ago, Stemen says, “customers had real concern about the lift.” Since then, “there’s more evidence of that working out, and the tools have improved, and the products have gotten better all at the same time.”

Alongside its general-purpose and memory-optimized VMs, Cobalt 200 brings two additional families to general availability: the high-memory Mpsv4 family, with 16 GiB of memory per vCPU, and the storage-optimized Lpsv5 family, with up to 23 TB of local NVMe storage.

“But now we’re seeing interest and desire for large in-memory databases, large existing enterprise workloads,” Stemen says, “and the ability to port them now being easier has helped.”

And while Microsoft will continue to invest in x86 chips, the company says it expects Cobalt 200 to make up “a significant portion of our new Azure Compute capacity in 2027 and moving forward.”

Developers can deploy the VMs through the existing Azure tools and use them in Virtual Machine Scale Sets or as Azure Kubernetes Service node pools.

The post Microsoft’s ARM-based Cobalt 200 chips go GA. Why it matters for AI agents. appeared first on The New Stack.
Microsoft’s Cobalt 200 Arm VMs are now generally available on Azure, with up to 50% more performance and tuning for the sandboxes AI agents run in.

item.title: Replit’s agent swarms built an app monitoring platform in 2 days on a $3K budget. Now, it’s offering them to customers.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Agent swarms are all the rage, as companies set about finding ways to coordinate multiple AI agents to tackle complex

The post Replit’s agent swarms built an app monitoring platform in 2 days on a $3K budget. Now, it’s offering them to customers. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Agent swarms are all the rage, as companies set about finding ways to coordinate multiple AI agents to tackle complex tasks in parallel.

In the past week alone, Google and Cursor unveiled competing approaches to multi-agent coding, building on existing efforts from companies including Anthropic, whose experimental Claude Code Agent Teams feature lets multiple agents collaborate on development tasks. OpenAI has also explored shared workspaces for agents.

On Tuesday, Replit revealed that it’s tapping deeper into the trend with Missions, a new product that lets users set objectives, establish budgets and approval requirements, and deploy swarms of AI agents to pursue them over hours, days, or even weeks.

How Replit Missions works

At its core, Missions is a way to delegate complex projects to AI agents, leaving them to determine how best to achieve a specified goal. Users establish the parameters through what Replit calls a Mission Agreement, which sets out success criteria, spending limits and actions requiring human approval.

To get started, users can type /mission in a conversation and describe their objective in plain English, such as getting every page on a website to load in under 500 milliseconds.

Crucially, users aren’t expected to devise a detailed plan upfront, giving agents the freedom to determine how best to approach a problem and adapt their methods as work progresses.

Replit president Michele Catasta says this is a very deliberate design choice, as requiring users to map out every step in advance could constrain the agents’ ability to find effective solutions.

“That would force the human to worry about implementation details, and not afford the flexibility the AI system might need to accomplish complex objectives.”

“That would force the human to worry about implementation details, and not afford the flexibility the AI system might need to accomplish complex objectives,” Catasta tells The New Stack.

A separate AI agent then evaluates the work against the agreed success criteria, sending it back for revisions if necessary before the user reviews the results.

The concept has parallels with other multi-agent tools, including Factory, which launched its own product called Missions earlier this year. Catasta argues that Replit’s approach differs in how it establishes user intent upfront, alongside the controls and infrastructure available to its agents.

For example, each agent operates in its own isolated cloud environment, with access to development tools, integrations and infrastructure such as databases, authentication and deployment.

Moreover, users must set a spending limit before a mission begins. Replit checks spending against that budget at every step, blocking further use of paid services once the limit is reached. Catasta argues that such controls are particularly important when multiple agents are operating autonomously.

“Most autonomous or multi-agent products lead to runaway token costs.”

“Most autonomous or multi-agent products lead to runaway token costs,” Catasta says.

Missions accomplished

Ahead of the launch, Replit says it used Missions to build Radar, its own application monitoring platform. According to the company, agents developed the system with direction from Replit engineers, completing it in two days with a $3,000 budget and producing dashboards, alerts and application tracing capabilities.

Replit then deliberately introduced a database fault to test the system, with Radar identifying the problem and raising an alert in 38 seconds, beating a 60-second target. In a separate three-hour test, the company says, it processed 26 million activity records and 4.4 million log entries without losing data.

While Radar was developed for Replit’s own use, the company eventually plans to release it to the public under an open-source license, following further reliability improvements and a code audit.

Additionally, Replit has tested Missions on software optimization, reporting speedups of up to 19 times across selected workloads in NumPy, the widely used open-source Python library for numerical computing, using 32-agent swarms.

Another internal example involved deploying 32 agents to improve Replit Slides, the company’s AI-powered presentation creation tool, with workers assigned different aspects of visual design and storytelling.

The company envisages broader applications, too, including researching potential enterprise customers, preparing tailored demonstrations, and refining sales outreach.

Keeping the swarm in check

While having multiple agents working in parallel sounds great in theory, it might raise concerns around the potential for duplicated work, conflicting code changes, spiralling costs, and the sheer difficulty of keeping autonomous systems under control.

To prevent agents from interfering with one another’s code, Replit draws on some of its existing technology, such as parallel Tasks. Its sandbox infrastructure allows agents to work on separate copies of a project before merging their changes, while a dedicated AI agent handles conflicts when those changes overlap. The same system, originally developed for collaboration between human developers, now supports agent swarms.

Moreover, improvements in the underlying AI models have also made this kind of coordination easier to execute.

“We’ve found that frontier models have gotten progressively better at splitting up work, and collaborating in parallel,” Catasta says. “Swarms have only started to be useful over the last few months as this behavior has been post-trained into the models.”

The appeal of this approach, ultimately, is that different agents can tackle different parts of a complex problem simultaneously, potentially completing work much faster than a single agent working sequentially. Catasta points to OpenAI’s recent work on the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, a longstanding mathematical challenge involving equations that describe fluid motion. OpenAI reported using approximately 10,000 coordinated agents to develop a proposed solution.

Catasta suggests that tackling such a problem could take centuries of human effort or years for a single agent, compared with weeks for a coordinated swarm. Those timelines are speculative, but they illustrate a broader argument for running many agents simultaneously.

“That’s because you can pack more compute and reasoning into a smaller amount of time by working in parallel in isolated environments, so long as you can have agents collaborate efficiently,” Catasta explains.

Replit also sees value in assigning different responsibilities to individual agents, much as a company brings together employees with different areas of expertise.

“This allows agents to focus their context on a particular part of the problem, rather than trying to make a single Agent manage context about many different subproblems simultaneously,” Catasta continues.

Of course, some tasks have inherent time constraints that additional workers cannot overcome — you can put ten cooks in a kitchen, but an egg still takes the same amount of time to boil. The same principle applies when a project has too few independent tasks to keep a large swarm occupied.

“There is a point of diminishing returns, both for time speedups and the benefit of specialization — you don’t want 500 agents making a 5 slide deck.”

“There is a point of diminishing returns, both for time speedups and the benefit of specialization — you don’t want 500 agents making a 5 slide deck,” Catasta says.

As such, the appropriate swarm size varies according to the complexity and nature of the assignment. “Replit is tuned to suggest an appropriate number of Agents for each job,” Catasta says.

There are also questions about how reliably autonomous agents respect the restrictions placed on them. In July 2025, a Replit coding agent deleted a customer’s production database despite instructions restricting its actions, prompting concerns about the risks of delegating consequential operations to AI.

Catasta maintains that incident “is still misunderstood,” noting that the affected Replit-managed database could be restored through the platform’s recovery tools. He says the company has since introduced more explicit controls governing which integrations agents can access and which actions require permission, with restrictions enforced at the infrastructure level.

“Anything not allowed is hard blocked by our proxy service,” Catasta says. “Replit is uniquely positioned to handle configurable agent security settings and isolate risk exposure by being in the cloud and being so mature within the enterprise.”

With Missions, Replit lets users set goals, budgets, and approval requirements, then deploy swarms of AI agents to tackle complex projects.

item.title: CoreWeave connects custom training loops to model serving
item.dc:creator: Urvashi Chowdhary
item.description:
Production traffic shows failures that benchmarks or pre-deployment evaluations can’t fully reveal. It tells you which edge cases matter and

The post CoreWeave connects custom training loops to model serving appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Production traffic shows failures that benchmarks or pre-deployment evaluations can’t fully reveal. It tells you which edge cases matter and what users need. Turning that signal into the next model version requires an upfront decision: does the model need to change, or is the problem in retrieval, context, prompts, tools, or serving?

Changing weights won’t fix a failure elsewhere in the system. When the model is the right place to intervene, production evidence can improve both quality and economics. A smaller model might reproduce a more expensive model’s behavior; better examples might improve consistency; an outcome-based reward might suit the task. Refining a capable model can also avoid another migration to a new model generation.

Choose a technique from the failure mode

Model distillation fits when a stronger model already produces the desired behavior and you want a smaller, more economical model to reproduce it. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) fits when high-quality examples can teach more consistent behavior. Reinforcement learning (RL) fits when you can reliably evaluate an outcome but cannot readily specify the ideal response in advance.

“Changing weights won’t fix a failure elsewhere in the system. When the model is the right place to intervene, production evidence can improve both quality and economics.”

You may use all three approaches over a model’s lifecycle. Choose from the evidence in your workload, even when that means using a technique that takes more setup.

Production traces have to become training data. Post-training needs compute and orchestration, and the resulting model has to be evaluated and returned to inference. That is the work of closing the loop. In RL, inference generates rollouts during training, and new weights must return to serving throughout the run.

At Fully Connected 2026, we introduced CoreWeave Model Distillation, CoreWeave RL Rollouts on CoreWeave Inference, and a programmable training API. These workflows connect in CoreWeave Forge. The programmable API is in limited preview, with an official launch planned for later in 2026.

Keep the data fresh when the base model stays

CoreWeave Model Distillation provides a managed workflow. CoreWeave Agent Lens captures inference traffic as the application runs. The workflow turns it into training data, relabels weak outputs, tests base models and hyperparameters, deploys candidates to Serverless Inference, and compares them with the production model.

If the model already has the capabilities your task needs, fresh production data can improve its fit without changing the serving profile you know. Compare the new version against the model already running before you move traffic.

Method used this workflow to revisit a model it had already deployed. In 2024, it used OpenPipe to train Llama 3.1 8B to navigate bank interactive voice response (IVR) systems, using GPT-4o outputs. In August 2026, Method brought in fresh production data, relabeled it with GPT-5.6 Sol, and trained another version. The candidate won 57.5% of head-to-head evaluations against the deployed version.

The base model had not changed. Fresh production data and Model Distillation in Forge made another iteration possible sooner. The 57.5% result is the share of head-to-head evaluations the new version won.

Control the training recipe in Python

For teams that want to design their own learning process, the programmable training API for Serverless Training separates training logic from infrastructure operations. You write a Python loop; CoreWeave manages the compute and underlying training infrastructure.

Here’s one way to combine RL updates with periodic supervised updates on verified demonstrations. The example creates a learner and serving adapter, uses an Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1e-5, and publishes updated weights to the sampler after each step.

Python
learner = await training.create_learner(model=model, lora=lora)
sampler = await serving.create_adapter(name="sampler")
optimizer = AdamConfig(learning_rate=1e-5)

for step in range(num_steps):
    trajectories = await run_agent(sampler, tasks)
    update = learner.batch()
    update.forward_backward(
        build_rl_batch(trajectories), loss="importance_sampling"
    )
    update.optim_step(optimizer=optimizer)

    if (step + 1) % sft_interval == 0:
        update.forward_backward(next_demo_batch(), loss="cross_entropy")
        update.optim_step(optimizer=optimizer)

    update.publish_weights(to=sampler)
    await update.result()

await (await learner.save_state("final")).result()
await learner.close()

The rollout and batch helpers are illustrative. Your agent logic, reward calculations, and data preparation belong in those helpers. The loop uses importance-sampling loss for RL and cross-entropy loss for demonstrations, then waits for the update result. It saves the final learner state and closes the learner.

You choose how often demonstrations enter the loop, how rewards are calculated, and how the recipe evolves. SFT, RL, and distillation share the training primitives, while the platform runs the distributed systems underneath.

Willow began with supervised learning, then added RL scorers to reduce filler words, improve readability, and remove self-corrected phrases. The scorers were combined into a reward function. Lawrence Liu, Willow’s chief technology officer and co-founder, reported better text styling, emoji handling, and responsiveness to commands than in the deployed model.

Remove checkpoint reload delays from RL

RL serving needs enough rollout generation, alignment with the policy being trained, and timely weight updates. The trainer, reward logic, and environment can stay where they are while CoreWeave Inference handles this part of the loop.

CoreWeave RL Rollouts is built on Nvidia Dynamo with vLLM support. When the trainer writes a checkpoint, the service hot-loads it into a live deployment while preserving in-flight requests and endpoint availability. It returns training metadata: token log probabilities (logprobs), token IDs, and expert routing for mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.

“When the trainer writes a checkpoint, the service hot-loads it into a live deployment while preserving in-flight requests and endpoint availability. Serving uses the trainer’s current policy weights, removing staleness and redeployment delays that would otherwise hold up the next batch of rollouts.”

Checkpoints can be full snapshots or incremental deltas, reducing synchronization after the first upload. Serving uses the trainer’s current policy weights, removing staleness and redeployment delays that would otherwise hold up the next batch of rollouts.

Measure quality and infrastructure separately

We validated the workflow with Nvidia and you.com by post-training Nvidia Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for web search. The run combined SFT and RL with you.com’s search tools inside the training loop.

BrowseComp accuracy increased from a 36.97% baseline to 45.45%, a reported 22.94% relative improvement. Average tool calls fell 30.24%. Separately, hot-loading checkpoints into a live deployment was approximately 15 times faster than traditional redeployment cycles.

Better search tooling, post-training refinement, and harness improvements worked together to improve accuracy and reduce tool calls. Hot-loading cut the time spent waiting for checkpoint synchronization. If you’re trying to make a smaller or more efficient model competitive with models an order of magnitude larger, that extra training time matters too.

Keep the model connected to its experiment

CoreWeave Forge connects production inference, training, and serving again. Model Distillation supplies a managed path. The programmable API lets researchers control the training loop without managing its infrastructure. RL Rollouts supports teams keeping their own trainer while using CoreWeave for rollout inference.

Models produced by serverless training return as tagged artifacts that can move into Serverless Inference without a separate registry handoff. Experiments remain logged beside them, keeping the run, model, and eventual deployment connected.

“Choose a failure you can reproduce, use it to guide the training method, and compare the candidate with the model serving users.”

Choose a failure you can reproduce, use it to guide the training method, and compare the candidate with the model serving users. Keep the production examples, evaluation, and resulting artifact together so your team can use them again.

The CoreWeave Forge blog and announcement press release provide context on the capabilities introduced at Fully Connected 2026. CoreWeave also plans further engineering explanations of Model Distillation, the programmable training API, and RL Rollouts.

item.title: AI agents were all over KubeCon. Production is another story
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
AI agents are testing systems that were originally built for people, and Jonathan Bryce thinks the cloud-native community has a

The post AI agents were all over KubeCon. Production is another story appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents are testing systems that were originally built for people, and Jonathan Bryce thinks the cloud-native community has a lot of work to do to help those systems keep up in this new era.

The New Stack sat down with Bryce, the executive director of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City to talk about the projects joining the foundation and how AI is changing its work.

Bryce tells The New Stack, “A lot of the existing systems in our world were built for human speed, and agent speed is a completely different type of usage pattern and scenario, and so these systems are just not scalable and resilient enough to handle the kind of workloads that agents are generating.”

Running training and inference workloads on Kubernetes is already a familiar job for this community, and Bryce argues that the financial services, healthcare, and transportation systems that agents interact with will also need the elasticity and observability that cloud-native technologies provide.

OpenShell and Agent Substrate

At KubeCon, Nvidia announced that it was contributing OpenShell to the CNCF. Google had also announced the donation of Agent Substrate ahead of the show. Both joined the CNCF as Sandbox projects, the foundation’s entry-level tier.

At its core, OpenShell enforces policies, including which files, networks, credentials, and model endpoints an agent can access. Agent Substrate tackles a related but different issue by providing isolated environments for agents on Kubernetes, with features like support for suspending idle sessions and resuming them when needed.

“We can make AI systems that have security and control architected into them from the infrastructure side,” Bryce says.

He sees this as a responsibility for the community, given the questions AI has raised about security and resource consumption. Moving a project like OpenShell into neutral governance also lets more companies contribute to it, he says.

Doing more with existing hardware

Agent workloads also aren’t as evenly distributed as those of more traditional enterprise applications.

“Your agent, even if it’s always waiting around to be at your beck and call, it’s not necessarily doing work 24/7,” Bryce says. “How do you spin it down and spin it up where it feels like it’s ready for you at any time? That’s going to be the user experience that people demand. How do you do that without just having it sit there and burn CPU cycles on nothing?”

Agent Substrate saves the agent’s state and frees up the compute it was using, then restores the session onto an available worker.

Bryce also highlighted llm-d, the distributed inference framework, as an example of software getting more out of existing hardware. While hardware is expensive, expensive to run, and (at least currently) in limited supply, software gives developers something they can work on now.

A flood of vulnerability reports

Zero-days and security also came up more at this KubeCon than in previous years.

As more people use AI tools to find and report vulnerabilities, Bryce says, open source maintainers have been flooded with duplicate and unverified reports that they still have to take seriously.

He thinks the pace may no longer be accelerating the way it was early this year, but he isn’t sure what 2027 will bring as the models keep getting better.

“Y2K didn’t end up being that big of a deal,” he says. “This is really a moment that could be a big deal if we don’t actually just all get together and work as quickly as we can.”

Agent adoption is still early

For all the talk about agents at the show, though, Bryce’s assessment of adoption is measured.

“Beyond software development, adoption is still quite low,” he says.

He sees production use in customer service and other areas with a well-defined, historical base of knowledge.

“We’re very, very, very early in the path to billions of agents that are taking action on our behalf on a constant basis,” Bryce says.

Companies remain cautious about what happens when they give an agent access and something goes wrong, which won’t come as a surprise if you’ve recently spent any time talking to big enterprises and their customers.

For now, Bryce sees this as a positive, because it may just allow the community enough time to harden projects like OpenShell and Agent Substrate before enterprises put agents to work more broadly.

The post AI agents were all over KubeCon. Production is another story appeared first on The New Stack.
At KubeCon, CNCF’s Jonathan Bryce says AI agents strain systems built for human speed and that adoption beyond coding is still very early.

item.title: Google found hackers using autonomous AI agents to turn security patches into exploits
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google’s Threat Intelligence Group says attackers are using autonomous AI agents to reverse-engineer security patches, generate exploits, and attempt to

The post Google found hackers using autonomous AI agents to turn security patches into exploits appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google’s Threat Intelligence Group says attackers are using autonomous AI agents to reverse-engineer security patches, generate exploits, and attempt to execute them without human approval.

In a report published Monday, Google and Mandiant describe the first cases their researchers have identified of attackers using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

The framework uses an orchestrator to coordinate specialized agents, share context, and invoke tools through interfaces such as MCP. The agents apply familiar coding workflows to offensive security, identifying vulnerabilities, generating exploit candidates, and testing them against targets.

Inside the exploit pipeline

Google found a publicly exposed staging server running a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent alongside stolen victim data and scripts used after a successful intrusion. The framework connected several frontier and locally hosted language models to automate patch diffing, turning potential vulnerabilities into exploit code that it could then attempt to execute.

The server also contained scripts for reconnaissance, brute-force attacks, installing webshells, and removing those left by competing attackers. Google found evidence that the operators were interested in French media, entertainment, and education websites, and that the framework had examined access controls in the Spectra WordPress plugin.

What’s changed is that agents can now do much of that work themselves.

Patch diffing is nothing new. Attackers have been comparing code before and after security patches for years to figure out what was fixed and how to exploit it. What’s changed is that agents can now do much of that work themselves.

Google didn’t identify which models handled individual tasks or disclose how often the generated exploits succeeded. And while the server contained stolen data, researchers couldn’t determine whether exploit_agent obtained it.

Agent harnesses go offensive

Google also found attackers using open-source offensive frameworks built around orchestration patterns familiar from coding agents.

CAIRN coordinates specialized agents through a shared blackboard and an observe-orient-decide-act loop, using the results of each task to determine what happens next. Google observed the framework in intrusions targeting U.S. aerospace organizations.

Other frameworks take different approaches. CyberStrikeAI uses a Go backend to orchestrate commercial and open-weight models across more than 100 security tools, YAML attack recipes, and custom scripts. HexStrike AI exposes more than 150 offensive security tools through MCP, with specialized agents handling reconnaissance, exploitation, and binary analysis.

Faster than patch cycles

Publicly available vulnerability information is also reaching attackers faster, leaving defenders less time to deploy fixes.

After two PaperCut vulnerabilities were exploited as zero-days in August, security researchers and Huntress developed working exploits with LLM assistance within a day of disclosure.

The attacker moved from initial access to domain administrator within minutes.

GreyNoise documented a campaign four days after the initial disclosure in which an attacker likely used language models to develop exploits, build target lists, and attack hundreds of organizations. The attacker moved from initial access to domain administrator within minutes.

Two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, presented a similar risk when patched code and a proof-of-concept video became public ahead of the official October 21 release.

Hundreds of purported exploits appeared online after the patches shipped, although many didn’t work and were likely generated with LLM assistance. Security teams then had to determine which exploits posed a real threat and which were simply nonfunctional code.

Velocity over stealth

These frameworks are still relatively easy to detect. Google found that they generate substantial network traffic and leave behind recognizable signatures and code artifacts. Researchers noted that attackers “currently trade stealth for velocity.”

The agents also hallucinate technical details and nonexistent targets, sometimes derailing attacks or exposing operators.

The agents also hallucinate technical details and nonexistent targets, sometimes derailing attacks or exposing operators.

For application security teams, the concern is how quickly attackers can move from a published patch to a working exploit.

The post Google found hackers using autonomous AI agents to turn security patches into exploits appeared first on The New Stack.
Google and Mandiant found attackers using autonomous AI agents to diff patches, write exploits, and run them, moving from disclosure to attack in minutes.

item.title: DuckDB 2.0 goes client-server and adds an Agent Mode for coding agents
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Riggins
item.description:
DuckDB has always been the database you don’t have to set up: Import it into your code and start querying.

The post DuckDB 2.0 goes client-server and adds an Agent Mode for coding agents appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
DuckDB has always been the database you don’t have to set up: Import it into your code and start querying. DuckDB 2.0 was released in October, and it can now run as a server that other machines can connect to. DuckLabs’ Gábor Szárnyas calls this the headline feature of the release.

The team decided to make this latest upgrade a major release since that feature, along with a new storage format and a new SQL parser, marks a big shift in how DuckDB works. On The New Stack podcast, Szárnyas explains what changed, what early users are teaching the team ahead of the 2.0.1 bug-fix release, and how to plan a production upgrade.

Codenamed Cinnamon Teal, DuckDB 2.0 is the analytical database’s biggest feature release to date, more than two years after 1.0.0.

We met with Szárnyas, head of developer relations at DuckLabs, at the company’s Amsterdam headquarters. DuckDB 2.0 can run as a server and query data faster.

“The other features are an extensible SQL parser, which was experimental earlier this year, but now is something that we turn on by default. That ideally doesn’t break anything, but it might,” Szárnyas says. “We also wanted to signify this with the release and the whole approach to doing more of a networked operation, shipping the Quack remote protocol as a first-class citizen in DuckDB.”

Database files created with DuckDB 2.0 can’t be opened by earlier versions, though 2.0 can still read and write existing database files, which stay readable by older versions. For production systems, Szárnyas repeats a common rule of thumb in the database world: “you should never migrate to a .0 release in production.” Depending on a team’s risk tolerance, he says, 2.0.1 or 2.0.2 is the version to move production to. The team is working on 2.0.1 now, focused on bug fixes, small performance tweaks and user feedback.

DuckDB 2.0.0 already includes dedicated Agent Mode, which makes it easier for AI coding agents to interpret errors and correct their own SQL queries, helping them get better results faster without wasting tokens. 

“The AI doesn’t really care. The large language models don’t mind if a text is formatted badly or the punctuation isn’t perfect.”

“For AI agents, we just print simple Markdown tables in compact mode with no spacing. The AI doesn’t really care. The large language models don’t mind if a text is formatted badly or the punctuation isn’t perfect,” Szárnyas says, which lets DuckDB “compress these tables down to maybe 60, 70% of their original size. It is just as legible for the agent.”

Agent Mode comes with no hidden truncation, machine-readable errors structured in JSON, and guardrails against runaway queries, and it works with coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

Following Amazon’s announcement to acquire DuckLabs in August, AWS shared how it uses the in-process analytical engine internally, including to query in S3 Tables. Mai-Lan Tomsen Bukovec, AWS’s technology VP, says AWS has processed more than 2.5 billion queries using its custom Quick query engine with DuckDB integrations and optimizations. She writes that DuckDB has helped Amazon Quick reduce average query latency by 30%.

DuckDB is also set to become the universal SQL dialect of AWS Storage and Analytics. In its Q3 earnings call in October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy remarked that this will simplify data processing with “a modern analytics engine that is fast, simple to use and ubiquitous, and where customers will be able to write SQL queries once and then execute using any AWS analytics service.” This includes zero migration or portability costs between query engines, which Jassy said will also help AI agents query data efficiently.

The post DuckDB 2.0 goes client-server and adds an Agent Mode for coding agents appeared first on The New Stack.
DuckLabs’ Gábor Szárnyas explains the new Quack protocol, Agent Mode and storage format, and how teams should plan a production upgrade.

item.title: Dax Raad rebuilt his browser tool in Rust for $60. Then memory use fell 97%.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenCode developer Dax Raad says he rebuilt the project’s browser automation tool in Rust for $60, replacing the parts of

The post Dax Raad rebuilt his browser tool in Rust for $60. Then memory use fell 97%. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenCode developer Dax Raad says he rebuilt the project’s browser automation tool in Rust for $60, replacing the parts of Playwright and Patchright it actually used and dramatically reducing its memory footprint.

A 4.3 MB binary

The figures he posted to X on Saturday are striking. The new Rust binary is just 4.3 MB, compared with 53 to 64 MB for the previous Node version. Memory use for each OpenCode Browse connector also fell from roughly 190 MB to 5.6 MB after a few calls, a reduction of about 97%.

The new Rust binary is just 4.3 MB, compared with 53 to 64 MB for the previous Node version.

The relay that wires AI coding agents to the browser shows a similar gap, with Raad’s comparison putting the Rust implementation at 6 MB idle, or 6.6 MB once it has served calls, against 353 MB for the old Node relay after six days of running.

Replacing Playwright and Patchright

OpenCode Browse connects AI coding agents to a developer’s existing browser through a Chromium extension and an MCP server. The previous Node implementation used Playwright for browser automation and Patchright to reduce detection, but Raad rebuilt the functionality Browse needed in Rust to cut runtime overhead.

Raad rebuilt the functionality Browse needed in Rust to cut runtime overhead.

The new Rust relay communicates with the Chromium extension over WebSockets and uses the Chrome DevTools Protocol to handle browser operations, agent sessions, recordings, and network captures. It also embeds QuickJS to execute agent-supplied JavaScript without requiring the previous Node runtime.

Inside the pull request

The merged pull request confirms that Raad replaced the Node-based CLI and relay while keeping the existing Chromium extension and using the Chrome DevTools Protocol for browser operations.

The team ran two rounds of testing with about 10 regression agents against a real Chrome browser. Browse scored 85% on Stealth Bench v2, compared with 90.5% for Browser Use Cloud, although the pull request doesn’t include a score for the old Node version.

Not everything made it into the rewrite; Raad dropped time zone and locale emulation along with the download tool, which Chrome blocks for extensions. The Rust version also retains a problem from the Node implementation where a busy-looping eval can’t be stopped through the extension.

Browse still includes relay authentication, extension pairing and origin restrictions, and agents are limited to tabs they open themselves or that users explicitly share with them.

The real $60 cost

Raad says the rewrite “only cost $60” and confirmed in a reply on X that he used Claude Opus as his main coding model and DeepSeek as a subagent.

The two models helped him replace the Playwright and Patchright functionality Browse needed, although the $60 figure doesn’t include the time he spent checking, testing, and fixing the code. The challenge with Rust rewrites is finding a smaller replacement that matches the original’s functionality without creating more maintenance work.

the $60 figure doesn’t include the time he spent checking, testing, and fixing the code

The memory savings are impressive, but Raad has also taken on responsibility for code that Playwright and Patchright previously maintained. His team will also have to deal with browser updates, authentication changes and security fixes that previously came through those libraries. That’s where AI-generated technical debt can become a problem, especially when code is cheap to produce but takes considerably more work to maintain.
