OpenCode developer Dax Raad rewrote the Browse automation tool in Rust for $60, cutting per-connector memory use by about 97% over the old Node version.

item.title: With Qwen4-Max, Alibaba puts the open source jacket back on the hanger
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Alibaba has officially unveiled Qwen4-Max, the first model in its next-generation Qwen4 family, with a focus on complex professional tasks

The post With Qwen4-Max, Alibaba puts the open source jacket back on the hanger appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Alibaba has officially unveiled Qwen4-Max, the first model in its next-generation Qwen4 family, with a focus on complex professional tasks and autonomous AI agents.

The Chinese tech titan teased the new Qwen4 family last week, taking to X to promise improvements in coding, reasoning and real-world knowledge, while initially making Qwen4-Max available in preview through several of its products.

Now, the company has formally detailed the model’s capabilities, pitching it as an always-available “AI teammate” capable of tackling everything from software development to scientific research.

However, Alibaba appears to be keeping its most powerful model proprietary, despite the open-weight releases that have helped establish Qwen as a major force in the AI realm.

Under the hood of Qwen4-Max

In a blog post published on Monday, Alibaba revealed that Qwen4-Max is built on a new mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture comprising 2.4 trillion backbone parameters, with 71 billion activated for each token. It also includes another 328 billion parameters dedicated to a technique called “N-gram Embedding,” which helps the model process patterns in text more efficiently.

The model supports images as well as text, and comes with a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process large amounts of information in a single interaction.

Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba’s QwenCloud platform, with API pricing starting at $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. It can also be accessed through QwenWork, Qoder and QwenStudio, while Vercel has added Qwen4-Max to its AI Gateway, allowing developers to use the model through coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

Alibaba claims the new architecture delivers substantial improvements over its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, particularly when performing complex tasks involving multiple tools and extended periods of autonomous execution.

On Work360, an internal benchmark developed to assess professional tasks across hundreds of specialised fields, Qwen4-Max scored 52.69 compared with 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Alibaba also claims the newer model uses between 24% and 35% fewer tokens on that benchmark, depending on the reasoning effort selected.

The company reports even greater token savings on Terminal-Bench 4.0, a test of AI agents’ ability to carry out tasks in a terminal environment, where token usage fell by nearly half compared with Qwen3.8-Max.

Alibaba says those improvements, combined with lower API prices, reduced the average cost of completing a task in its Work360 evaluation by 62%, from $4.43 to $1.67.

Of course, those are Alibaba’s own results. Independent testing by Artificial Analysis offers another perspective, awarding Qwen4-Max a score of 43 on its Intelligence Index, placing it 38th among 81 models in the comparison. That puts it slightly above the median score of 41 for models in its price category, but lagging leading competitors such as Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 (65), Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon (60) and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra (57).

Artificial Analysis also calculated an average cost of $3.27 per task across its evaluations, while noting that Qwen4-Max generated 127 million output tokens, considerably more than the median of 78.6 million among comparable models.

Alibaba pulls its weight(s)

The proprietary nature of Qwen4-Max is particularly notable given Alibaba’s recent history. When the company introduced Qwen3.8-Max in August, it made an unusual commitment: for the first time, it would release the weights underlying one of its flagship Max models, allowing developers to download and run a version on their own infrastructure.

That marked a departure from Alibaba’s previous approach, with Qwen3.6-Max-Preview and Qwen3.7-Max both remaining proprietary. In hindsight, Qwen3.8-Max looks more like an exception than the beginning of a broader shift towards open weights.

The announcement followed Alibaba’s efforts to demonstrate that its models could compete with leading proprietary systems from the likes of Anthropic. As The New Stack reported at the time, the company had already been making increasingly ambitious performance claims for its Qwen family.

Qwen3.8-Max also arrived with a demonstration of autonomous software development, in which an AI coding agent worked on a project over 16 days, producing hundreds of commits and more than 100 pull requests.

However, the open-weight promise initially attracted scepticism when Alibaba announced the model release before making the files available.

“That is not a technical footnote; that is the API business model wearing an open source jacket for the launch photo.”

In reactions gathered by The New Stack, independent AI consultant Jeff Brokaw questioned the significance of advertising downloadable weights that developers could not yet obtain. He also drew parallels with Chinese AI startup Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, which had similarly been promoted as an open-weight model ahead of the files becoming available.

“That is not a technical footnote; that is the API business model wearing an open source jacket for the launch photo,” Brokaw said at the time.

Alibaba, for its part, did eventually follow through on August 12, publishing the underlying Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B weights — but there were notable strings attached. The downloadable model came under a custom licence, versus the more permissive Apache 2.0 terms Alibaba had used for various earlier Qwen releases. Businesses operating “model-as-a-service” or AI work assistant products, with combined revenue exceeding $50 million over any consecutive 12-month period, were required to obtain a separate commercial licence, although internal use was exempt under specified conditions.

The licence also required certain commercial products with more than 100 million monthly active users, or $20 million in monthly revenue, to prominently display the model’s name.

For comparison, Xiaomi released its MiMo-V2.6 models under the permissive MIT licence in September, alongside technical documentation and a public record of its reinforcement-learning training costs. The company also committed to publishing thousands of training environments and associated tools, giving outside developers a potentially deeper view of how the models were developed.

Alibaba was willing to wear the “open source jacket,” while keeping some of its most valuable capabilities behind a commercial API. And with Qwen4-Max, the company appears to be putting that jacket back on the hanger.

The released Qwen3.8-Max weights also represented a more limited version of the hosted product, lacking some of the capabilities available through Alibaba’s API, including native image input.

In other words, Alibaba was willing to wear the “open source jacket,” while keeping some of its most valuable capabilities behind a commercial API. And with Qwen4-Max, the company appears to be putting that jacket back on the hanger completely — no downloadable weights have been announced for the new model, and Alibaba has made no commitment to publish them.

On X and the accompanying blog post, Alibaba did say that the “open weights of smaller Qwen4 models will be released,” although it has yet to specify which models or when they will become available. But for Qwen4-Max itself, developers remain reliant on Alibaba’s hosted services or third-party API providers.

The post With Qwen4-Max, Alibaba puts the open source jacket back on the hanger appeared first on The New Stack.
After opening Qwen3.8-Max, Alibaba is back to its old playbook: Qwen4-Max is API-only. But smaller Qwen4 models will eventually get open weights.

item.title: DuckDB has an answer to “bloated” database messages
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Riggins
item.description:
Older database protocols were built before big data. Some still send results row by row, repeating details like column names

The post DuckDB has an answer to “bloated” database messages appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Older database protocols were built before big data. Some still send results row by row, repeating details like column names and types with every row. The result, says DuckLabs product team lead Guillermo Sánchez Dionis, is “quite a bloated message.” That overhead adds up when you’re moving large query results.

DuckDB’s answer is Quack, an HTTP-based protocol that streams query results in batches of column data as DuckDB produces them. It was previewed in May and was released in October as part of DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS.

On this latest episode of The New Stack podcast, recorded at DuckLabs headquarters in Amsterdam, Sánchez Dionis explains how that design lets developers start working with results while a query is still running.

A database protocol is a formal set of rules and message formats that dictates how a client application communicates with a database server. It acts as a specialized language that lets a software application securely send SQL queries, receive structured data tables, and manage transactions over a network. It handles connection and authentication, query packaging, data serialization, and error management. 

But according to Sánchez Dionis, most protocols were designed pre-big data for other types of systems, with serialized rows rather than columns. They also add a lot of unnecessary data, he says, like column types and column names per row.

“It becomes quite a bloated message. That already makes the protocol not only not good for analytical systems, but it’s also quite heavy,” he contends. As protocols evolved for analytical systems, they did start using columns, but “they were still doing things like serializing one value at a time and other things that are really not efficient. Modern systems are trying to converge on using vectorized execution to be able to serialize more values at a time and trying to use more efficient representations of columnar data formats to send over the wire.”

All while the Quack protocol, he says, is aiming for a different, highly efficient approach.

Quack is DuckDB’s HTTP-based client/server protocol, with its first production release shipping in DuckDB 2.0.0 on Oct. 21. Not only does this signal Quack moving out of the preview stage, but the protocol now offers certain developer-friendly features:

  • The CONNECT statement allows developers to attach to and query a remote Quack server via standard SQL commands.
  • The new -serve CLI argument instantly starts a Quack server instance from the command line, and -connect connects to one.
  • Multiple clients can write to the same database concurrently, with transactions handled under DuckDB’s multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) isolation.

“Quack uses DuckDB’s data chunks — which is our columnar representation of data. We also serialize in a very efficient manner because we are a vectorized engine. We also make sure that we send the results in a streaming fashion,” Sánchez Dionis explains. 

“One of the most important things is tightly coupling the engine. Once you start producing results, instead of waiting for the query execution to end and then serializing all of the results at once, you serialize and send results as they are emitted by the engine. Therefore, the client can keep consuming results without having to stop the engine.”

For developers, he says, that means they don’t have to do anything. 

“I think the biggest advantage that you will see is you will have a very small memory footprint”

“You run a query from the comfort of your laptop, and you just get streaming results back. I think the biggest advantage that you will see is you will have a very small memory footprint,” he says. “What’s cool about Quack is that you install and load it wherever you are. You can also create another client on the [same] laptop with the Quack extension, and they will communicate with each other.”

Then, the scale of how many DuckDB servers is up to you and your team. And the overhead of running it on that server is next to none, Sánchez Dionis continues, as it’s Quack’s biggest efficiency gain yet.

More Quack improvements are expected in upcoming DuckDB 2.0 patch releases, as the DuckLabs team looks to build stability on the server side.

The post DuckDB has an answer to “bloated” database messages appeared first on The New Stack.
Why do some database protocols still send column names with every row? DuckLabs’ Guillermo Sánchez Dionis tells us how DuckDB’s Quack fixes that.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Opus 5.5: Same scores at almost 4x the cost
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9 and said it beats Claude Opus 5.5 in almost every capability the

The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Opus 5.5: Same scores at almost 4x the cost appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9 and said it beats Claude Opus 5.5 in almost every capability the company measured. In the same announcement, it recommended starting with Opus for most coding and knowledge tasks, calling it its “strongest daily driver.” I wanted to find out why a company would steer people away from its best model, and whether the cheaper one really is enough.

…why a company would steer people away from its best model, and whether the cheaper one really is enough.

On Anthropic’s coding benchmarks, Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% at Xhigh effort on FrontierCode 2.0, compared with 45.5% for Opus 5.5 at Max. Anthropic also reports that Fable scored 45.3% at High effort at roughly half the cost per task of that Opus run. On FrontierSWE v2, the company reports 69.9% for Fable and 62.3% for Opus. Fable’s standard API rates are twice Opus’s: $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, versus $4 and $20.

Twice the price should make a meaningful difference, so I gave both models three coding and agent jobs and measured how well they did, how many tokens they used, what they cost, and how long they took. My tests are much smaller than Anthropic’s benchmarks and can’t prove or disprove those scores. 

The tests

I ran each model once per test through Anthropic’s API at default settings, with no turn cap. Anthropic’s API defaults on Fable and Opus aren’t equal. Fable 5.2 runs at high effort, and Opus 5.5 runs at medium, so these results show what a developer gets without tuning anything. I used a script to grade each answer the model gave for each test. The dollar figures are estimated API costs based on reported token usage. Anthropic prices uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output separately.

Here are the tests I ran:

  • Cron scheduler: I gave each model a written spec for code that runs when the next scheduled job runs, then sent a change request. I used a hidden suite of 50 tests to grade the final code.
  • Invoicing repo fix: Each model worked as an agent in a small invoicing library with interacting bugs in rounding, discounts, tax, and shipping. The library also had one wrong test that the model should report but not edit.
  • Incident investigation: Each model used a terminal to find the cause of a payments outage from logs, metrics, and deployment records. The data included decoy deploys and servers with wrong clocks.

The models tied with perfect scores on the first version of every test, so I made each test harder and reran it twice.

Cron scheduler

This test checks whether a model can turn a detailed spec into correct code and then absorb a change without breaking it. Here’s what differed between the versions.

  • Version 1: The spec covered standard cron schedules, such as every 15 minutes or weekdays at 9 a.m.
  • Version 2: I added rules like “the weekday nearest the 15th” and “the last Friday of the month,” and the change request reversed how two fields combine.
  • Version 3: The code had to handle time zones and daylight saving time by hand, without Python’s time zone library.

Both models scored 50/50 on all three versions. The difference was in how much work each one did to get there. Fable 5.2 wrote two to three times as much reasoning as Opus 5.5 on every version. The extra reasoning did not raise Fable’s score on any of the three versions.

The extra reasoning did not raise Fable’s score on any of the three versions.

Across the three scheduler versions, Opus matched Fable’s scores in 358 seconds versus 661 and cost an estimated $0.99 versus $3.29.

The numbers:

  • Version 1
    • Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 14,471 in, 18,732 out (11,122 reasoning), $0.87, 170 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 2 turns, 8,055 in, 9,431 out (3,846 reasoning), $0.22, 80 s.
  • Version 2
    • Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 20,215 in, 23,990 out (14,627 reasoning), $1.12, 226 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 2 turns, 14,090 in, 15,991 out (6,695 reasoning), $0.38, 131 s.
  • Version 3
    • Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 21,121 in, 28,254 out (17,452 reasoning), $1.30, 265 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 2 turns, 12,651 in, 17,205 out (6,533 reasoning), $0.39, 147 s.

Invoicing repo fix

This bug hunt is similar to the work agents do for developers daily. Here’s how I adjusted the tests with each round:

  • Version 1: The library had bugs in rounding, discounts, tax, and shipping. It also had one wrong test.
  • Version 2: I added buy-two-get-one promotions, weight-based shipping, and refunds, each with its own bugs.
  • Version 3: I added currency conversion and invoice numbering, again with bugs.

This test produced the widest gap in cost and time between the two models. Both models scored 50 of 50 on all three versions, fixing the bugs the grader covered and reporting the wrong test without editing it. Opus 5.5 used fewer reasoning tokens on every version. It finished each version in under a minute, while Fable 5.2 took about one minute and 46 seconds to just under four minutes and cost eight times as much across the three.

On these runs, Fable’s extra reasoning didn’t improve its score.

The numbers:

  • Version 1
    • Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 17,585 in, 11,511 out (5,909 reasoning), $0.58, 106 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 4 turns, 10,585 in, 2,975 out (519 reasoning), $0.09, 28 s.
  • Version 2
    • Fable 5.2: 6 turns, 88,697 in, 25,980 out (11,820 reasoning), $1.39, 223 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 4 turns, 13,938 in, 4,457 out (777 reasoning), $0.13, 39 s.
  • Version 3
    • Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 29,660 in, 24,020 out (14,022 reasoning), $1.18, 214 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 5 turns, 24,208 in, 6,013 out (1,178 reasoning), $0.17, 51 s.

Incident investigation

This test rewards careful digging more than fast coding, so I expected it to favor Fable 5.2.

Here are the changes I made for each test version.

  • Version 1: The outage data had decoy deploys and one server whose clock ran seven minutes slow.
  • Version 2: I added a clock that was corrected partway through the incident, retried requests, a compressed log file, and duplicated log lines.
  • Version 3: I added a server that logged in Chicago time and an unrelated error spike inside the incident window.

Both models scored perfectly (50 out of 50) across all three versions. Fable 5.2 took fewer turns in every version, 9 to 11 versus Opus 5.5’s 12 to 14. Across all three versions, Fable’s estimated cost was $2.54 versus Opus’s $0.91.

The numbers:

  • Version 1
    • Fable 5.2: 9 turns, 155,925 in, 14,309 out (8,638 reasoning), $0.94, 143 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 12 turns, 111,618 in, 7,405 out (2,801 reasoning), $0.25, 73 s.
  • Version 2
    • Fable 5.2: 11 turns, 168,913 in, 9,416 out (3,551 reasoning), $0.68, 105 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 13 turns, 188,846 in, 7,218 out (2,518 reasoning), $0.32, 82 s.
  • Version 3
    • Fable 5.2: 10 turns, 205,601 in, 11,887 out (4,474 reasoning), $0.92, 127 s.
    • Opus 5.5: 14 turns, 253,958 in, 7,598 out (2,041 reasoning), $0.34, 70 s.

Results

The scores were identical across all nine runs per model. Fable 5.2 cost almost four times as much and took more than twice as long.

What do I think?

These tests give me a reason to start with Opus 5.5 for work like this. It matched Fable 5.2’s score and finished faster on every version, at about a quarter of the estimated cost overall.

That doesn’t make Fable 5.2 a bad model. My tests were hard but short. Anthropic recommends Fable for more open-ended technical work. I tested each model at its API default, so the comparison leaves open how much of the gap comes from the different effort settings.

I’d start with Opus 5.5 and move up to Fable 5.2 only when Opus stops producing ideal results.

The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Opus 5.5: Same scores at almost 4x the cost appeared first on The New Stack.
Anthropic says Fable 5.2 beats Opus 5.5 yet tells developers to start with Opus. In hands-on tests, Opus matched Fable’s scores at a quarter of the cost.

item.title: AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part.
item.dc:creator: Arjun Iyer
item.description:
This week, Amazon Web Services released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. It

The post AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
This week, Amazon Web Services released AWS Emulator, a local copy of AWS that coding agents can test against. It covers more than 200 AWS services and was written entirely by agents. The most useful part of the launch is a story Swami Sivasubramanian tells in the announcement.

About 20 years ago, Sivasubramanian helped build the replication engine inside Alf, a Paxos-based lock service that still powers AWS systems such as S3 and DynamoDB. The first build took about four months. When he later asked Kiro, AWS’s agentic coding tool, to rebuild it, he supervised the agent for four nights before he saw the problem: The agent had no way to check its own results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.

Same agent, same task. Four nights became two hours because the feedback loop changed.

“An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against.”

As Sivasubramanian puts it, distributed systems are hard to test. That matches what I see across teams running coding agents on production systems. An agent is only as good as its verification loop, and a verification loop is only as good as what it runs against. AWS Emulator solves that for the AWS APIs your code calls. It does not solve it for the services your team owns, and that is where most agent-written changes break.

AWS puts infrastructure inside the agent’s loop

A coding agent works in a loop. It writes code, runs it, reads the result, and decides what to change next. Sivasubramanian’s point is that in distributed systems, that loop runs inside infrastructure. If the services the code calls do not behave like the real ones, the agent learns the wrong lesson and keeps going.

AWS Emulator puts AWS into that loop on a laptop. Point existing AWS tools and code at it with one environment variable, and tests run against emulated services without changes.

Autonomous agents wrote every line of the emulator, working from AWS’s public API models. Each behavior is pinned by a fidelity test that first passes against real AWS, then against the emulator, and every change passes a merge gate where security agents review it. Sivasubramanian’s conclusion is that when agents write the code, the engineer’s job is to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when the work is correct.

The first reactions on Hacker News went straight to trust. One commenter counted roughly 30,000 commits in three weeks and questioned the quality. That is a fair question aimed at the wrong thing. Who wrote the code tells you little. What it was verified against tells you a lot, and AWS’s answer is real AWS.

“Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.”

What changed is who runs the loop. A developer checks a change a few times a day, and an agent checks it on every iteration. Slow or unrealistic feedback was a tax on people. For agents, it decides whether the loop works at all.

Every loop runs against mocks, an emulator, or the running system

An agent can verify its work against one of three things, and each has a different weakness.

Mocks are the weakest option, and AI has made them cheap. One Hacker News commenter argued that it is now faster to have AI mock your APIs, adding that “AI has been a boon for test coverage.” But an agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not.

Emulators are a real step up. AWS Emulator is checked against real AWS, so its behavior comes from the service rather than from the agent.

An emulator is still a model, though, and AWS is open about that. The repository keeps a folder of behaviors the agents found that do not match real AWS yet, and operations that are not implemented return an error instead of a fake success. An IDC analyst noted that at launch the emulator does not simulate throttling, outages, or per-Region availability, which is where retry and failover logic gets exercised.

“An agent that writes its own mocks writes them to match its own assumptions. The tests pass because they were built to pass, so coverage goes up while confidence should not.”

Sivasubramanian says as much about his own work on Alf. Simulation ironed out most of its concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing on real servers then turned up different problems, because “the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.”

You can’t emulate your own system the way AWS emulated its own

In the same HN thread, a self-described Amazonian outlined the approach most teams take with agents today: Close off as much of the system as possible, mock or simulate the dependencies that cannot be closed off, then let the agent loose. That works when the part you cannot close off is a cloud API with a published spec. It breaks down when that part is your own system.

AWS Emulator works because AWS had two things most teams will never have for their own software: a complete, machine-readable spec of every operation and a stable reference to check against in real AWS.

Now picture a payments platform with 60 microservices. The contracts between those services live in code, in a few OpenAPI files that drifted months ago and in the heads of the engineers who wrote them. There is no single spec, and the reference implementation is the running system itself, which changes every time someone merges. With agents opening pull requests (PRs) multiple times a day, it changes faster than any model of it could keep up with.

That is also where agent-written application code tends to break. The failures are rarely about how a managed queue handles a visibility timeout. They are a field renamed in one service that a consumer two teams away still reads, an event payload a downstream service does not expect, a query that is fast on fixtures and slow on production-sized data, or configuration, feature flags and secrets that only exist in the cluster. No emulator of a cloud provider will ever see them.

The environment belongs on the engineer’s list

Sivasubramanian lists specs, tests, and merge gates as the engineer’s job now. I would add the environment, because it decides what the agent can catch.

A realistic loop has six properties. The change runs in a production-like environment, next to the services, data, and configuration it will ship into. Each change gets its own isolated environment, so 10 agents working in parallel do not step on each other. The environment starts in seconds, because an agent that waits 20 minutes stops using it and the loop collapses back to unit tests. And the agent creates the environment and reads results itself, without filing a ticket.

The loop also runs the integration and end-to-end suites the team already trusts, not tests the agent wrote to agree with itself. And it produces evidence a reviewer or merge gate can act on before the change merges.

The hard part is getting production-like fidelity and fast startup at the same time. Cloning a full stack for every change buys fidelity and loses on speed and cost. A team of 10 engineers running multiple parallel agent sessions might produce 100 PRs a day or more that need to be verified. No team can justify the cost of 100+ full copies of the system.

Emulate what you don’t own, and run what you own for real

Emulators and production-like environments are not competing ideas. They are layers in the same loop.

For managed cloud services with published contracts, an emulator gives agents fast, free feedback on a laptop. If a service writes to S3 and reads from a queue, AWS Emulator catches API misuse in seconds without touching an AWS account.

“Emulators and production-like environments are not competing ideas. They are layers in the same loop.”

For the system you own, deploy only what the change modifies instead of cloning the stack. Requests and messages tagged for that change’s environment reach the new versions, and everything else is served by the shared stable environment that is already running. Databases and queues get lightweight per-environment schemas or topics only where the change needs data isolation. That is how an environment starts in seconds and still behaves like production. Uber and Lyft built internal systems on this model for the same reason.

Then make the merge gate ask for both. A PR that passed against an emulator and against the system it is joining is one a reviewer can trust.

Every agent will have a loop, and realism is what separates them

Sivasubramanian’s agent went from four nights to two hours once it could check its own work. For application teams, the next jump depends on what it checks against. An emulator covers the cloud APIs you call, and only the running system covers the services you own.

Having a verification loop is now expected. The realism of that loop is what decides how much you can trust the code that comes out of it. If you want your agents verifying every change in a production-like environment before merge, we built Signadot to make that the default.

The post AWS Emulator proves agents need a verification loop. Realism is the hard part. appeared first on The New Stack.
AWS Emulator proves coding agents need realistic verification loops—emulate cloud APIs you don't own, and run your services for real.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 promises fewer refusals and lower token prices, but those changes played out very differently in our

The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 promises fewer refusals and lower token prices, but those changes played out very differently in our head-to-head coding comparisons.

Anthropic compared Fable 5.2 with its predecessor, Fable 5.1, on safeguard blocks, output speed, and API pricing. The company states that Fable 5.2 triggered about 55% fewer safeguard blocks than Fable 5.1 overall and about 60% fewer in cybersecurity in early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork. It also says Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster and lists standard API rates of $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Both rates are 20% lower than Fable 5.1’s $10 and $50.

I compared Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1 on three developer tasks and tracked refusals, accuracy, tokens, estimated cost, and elapsed time. The comparison uses one run per model for each task or version, including the October Fable 5.1 webhook result. That’s a small sample, and the API runs used a different setup from Anthropic’s safeguard testing.

The tests

For the new runs, I used Anthropic’s API with the default effort setting of High for both models, with no turn cap or fallback model. A script graded every run against an answer key I created for the tests. The dollar figures are estimated API costs. Anthropic prices uncached input, cache reads, cache writes, and output separately.

  • Webhook chat: I reused a 50-turn scripted chat that I first ran on Fable 5.1 in October. It simulates a dev lead building a small webhook relay. The chat contains 25 project rules, eight of which change later and three of which are only implied. At the end, the model writes the config and code and then takes an eight-question recall quiz.
  • Signature checker: I gave each model a written spec for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders, and then sent a change request. A hidden suite of 50 tests graded the final code output.
  • Login repo fix: Each model worked as an agent in a small login library with interacting bugs in passwords, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. The library also had one wrong test that the model should report but not edit. 

Webhook chat

In the October Fable 5.1 run I’m using for comparison, the API refused 34 of 50 turns. The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. In that October run, I kept my prompts in the chat history and discarded refused model responses. Fable 5.1 also refused the final code and the quiz, so it scored zero on both. The task was to build an ordinary backend relay.

The first refusal came on turn 5, when I asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable.

Fable 5.2 finished the same script without a refusal. That gave me a complete run to grade for long-conversation recall. Its code used the most recent version of all eight rules, which changed midway, and on the quiz it answered “unknown” to the three questions that had no answer. Fable 5.2 didn’t fill gaps with guesses. 

The numbers:

• Fable 5.2: 50 turns, 298,709 in, 41,828 out (28,550 reasoning), $4.06, 427 s.

• Fable 5.1 (October): 34 of 50 turns refused, with no code or quiz answers.

Signature checker

Fable 5.1 refused both turns of this test in under a second each, and the API labeled both refusals “cyber.” The spec asked for code that verifies signed webhooks, rejects replays, and rate-limits senders. The API returned no output on either turn. Anthropic says benign security work can trigger its cyber classifier.

Fable 5.2 took the same spec, handled the change request, and passed all 50 hidden tests, including the edge cases on timestamps, rotated secrets, and replays.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 2 turns, 21,299 in, 26,167 out (18,407 reasoning), $1.22, 253 s.
  • Fable 5.1: 2 turns, both refused, 3,206 reported input tokens, 0 output tokens, $0.00 under Anthropic’s billing rules for cyber refusals before output, 2 s.

Login repo fix

This was the one test where both models completed the work, showing how they compare once refusals are out of the picture. The models kept getting perfect scores, so I made the tests harder and reran them twice. Here’s what differed between the tests:

  • Version 1: The library had bugs in four modules that handle password hashing, lockouts, reset tokens, and sessions. It also had one wrong test.
  • Version 2: I added a one-time-code module with its own bugs and tightened the rules in the existing modules. Usernames had to match across Unicode forms, and sessions had to handle a clock that runs backward.
  • Version 3: I added an audit log that must redact secrets and a rate limiter. Neither module came with any tests.

The models tied on all three versions of the login repo fix. Both scored 50/50 on each version, fixing the bugs the grader covered and reporting the wrong test without editing it.

Fable 5.1 never refused on the login repo fix, even though the task covered passwords, lockouts, and reset tokens.

Across the three versions, dividing total output tokens (including reasoning) by total elapsed time gives about 107 tokens per second for Fable 5.2 and 82 for Fable 5.1. The elapsed time includes the entire task run. Fable 5.2 took four turns on each version, while Fable 5.1 took 7, 21, and 25. Fable 5.2 also produced more reasoning tokens on each version. 

Fable 5.2 finished the first two versions faster and at a lower estimated cost. It took longer and cost more on the third.

The numbers:

  • Version 1
    • Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 16,149 in, 4,502 out (1,178 reasoning), $0.27, 43 s.
    • Fable 5.1: 7 turns, 33,935 in, 4,761 out (1,149 reasoning), $0.36, 52 s.
  • Version 2
    • Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 24,081 in, 10,024 out (4,887 reasoning), $0.56, 95 s.
    • Fable 5.1: 21 turns, 139,189 in, 9,475 out (4,018 reasoning), $0.68, 118 s.
  • Version 3
    • Fable 5.2: 4 turns, 34,269 in, 17,964 out (10,578 reasoning), $0.96, 166 s.
    • Fable 5.1: 25 turns, 208,826 in, 10,638 out (4,342 reasoning), $0.79, 132 s.

Results

The token, cost, and time totals below cover the signature checker and all three login repo versions. Fable 5.1 produced no output on the signature checker, while Fable 5.2 spent 253 seconds and an estimated $1.22 completing it. Across the three login versions that both models completed, elapsed time and estimated cost were close. The combined totals include the work only Fable 5.2 completed on the signature checker.

What do I think?

In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals. Fable 5.1 blocked ordinary webhook and signature-checking work, and Fable 5.2 completed both without a single refusal. Anthropic says the newer model still uses cyber safeguards.

In my tests, the biggest improvement with Fable 5.2 was fewer refusals.

Across the three login repo versions, Fable 5.2 produced about 30% more output tokens per second of elapsed time, including reasoning, while taking about the same total time. The runs took 304 seconds in total on Fable 5.2 and 302 seconds on Fable 5.1.

The displayed cost estimates add up to $1.79 and $1.83, respectively, a savings of about 2% for these runs. Anthropic’s 20% price cut applies to its standard per-token rates. I ran each version once per model, so I’d try both on your own workload to see what the numbers look like for you.

The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. Fable 5.1: Fewer refusals, with small savings on the login fix appeared first on The New Stack.
Claude Fable 5.2 stopped refusing ordinary webhook and security code in our tests. Its 20% price cut barely moved the bill once both models finished.

item.title: Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer
item.dc:creator: Bonnie Chase
item.description:
AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search

The post Web search for agents is here: Why ranking still decides the answer appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI agents have had a URL problem for a while. When an agent needs current information but has no search tool, it often makes up the web address it thinks the answer lives at. It might guess something like docs.example.com/v4.2/auth, try to load it, and get a “page not found” error because the page doesn’t exist. Then it either keeps guessing or falls back on outdated information from its training.

“Live web search gives AI agents fresh pages. Deciding which ones to trust over your own data is still a ranking problem.”

Infrastructure providers have noticed. In October, InfoQ reported that Cloudflare opened a beta Web Search API in its AI Gateway. Agents can call several search providers through one interface and get live results back with source links, logging, and access controls attached. Cloudflare’s reasoning was refreshingly direct: Without search, agents tend to guess.

This is a welcome change, and live search will probably be a default agent tool within a year, but it solves only the finding part of the problem. Once fresh pages are in front of an agent, something still has to decide which of those pages, and which of your own documents, the agent should actually rely on. That decision lives in your retrieval layer.

The problem: two pools of evidence, one context window

An agent working inside a company rarely answers from the web alone. It also has the data that makes it useful to that company: product catalogs, documentation, contracts, support history, account records,s and permissions. With web search wired in, every step of a task can now pull from two very different pools.

The agent has to reconcile these, often several times within one task. And the questions it needs answered are ones a search API was never built to handle. When yesterday’s vendor changelog contradicts an internal knowledge base article from last spring, which one wins? Does this result apply to this customer’s version and region? Is the agent even allowed to show it?

Those are ranking and filtering decisions. They depend on your data and business rules, so you have to make them where both are available.

Why concatenating results breaks in production

The simplest integration is to run a web search, run an internal search, append one list to the other, and let the model sort it out. It may work well at first, but once it’s running against growing data and traffic, it tends to fail in a few predictable ways:

  • Conflicts go unresolved. The model sees two confident sources that disagree and has no signal for which is newer or more authoritative, so it picks one or blends them into an answer that matches neither. 
  • Staleness hides. A 3-month-old knowledge base article that matches the user’s wording almost exactly will beat a 4-day-old changelog on similarity alone. Nothing in the embedding says the article is out of date. 
  • Permissions are applied too late. If access rules run after retrieval, restricted content may already be in the prompt. If they run crudely, useful results get dropped along with sensitive ones. 
  • Cost and latency compound. A person runs one search and reads the results. An agent can trigger a dozen or more retrieval calls in a single task as it plans, checks, and refines. Sending every candidate to the model on every call adds up quickly, and more context doesn’t reliably produce better answers.

A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does. 

“A bigger context window doesn’t fix any of these. Sending the model fewer, better-chosen pieces of evidence does.”

Clarm, a Y Combinator company that builds sales and support agents for open-source software companies, hit this early. Its founder, Marcus Storm-Mollard, said the team realized “search, not generation, was the real problem to solve.” Generating an answer was the easy part. Finding the right information to ground it in was the hard part, which is why Clarm runs text search, vector similarity, and structured filters through a single query instead of stitching separate stores together.

What changes when agents search across sources

When agents combine live web results with internal data, they need to account for different retrieval methods, metadata, permissions, and ranking signals. Four design considerations stand out.

1. Retrieve across methods in one query 

Keyword matching catches exact product names, error codes, and version strings, which embeddings are notoriously bad at. Vector search catches paraphrases and intent. Structured filters enforce hard constraints like customer, version, and entitlement.  

Within a single indexed collection, hybrid retrieval can combine keyword matching, vector similarity, and structured filters. That does not, by itself, fuse results from an external web search API with results from an internal index. The two-source integration requires a separate design decision.

select * from evidence where
  ({targetHits: 200}nearestNeighbor(embedding, q) or userQuery())
  and visibility contains "customer"
  and product_version contains "4.2"

The broader lesson is that retrieval systems need to handle lexical matching, semantic similarity, and filtering together. These requirements matter regardless of the search platform chosen. Perplexity hit this wall when it set out to build search in-house for its answer engine. Its CEO, Aravind Srinivas, has summed up the company’s approach as “first solve search, then solve everything else.” But when the team evaluated existing tools, it found that vector databases couldn’t reliably support even simple Boolean filters, while traditional search backends offered only primitive semantic ranking. It needed lexical retrieval, semantic retrieval, and filtering in one engine, at consumer scale, and chose Vespa to build it.

2. Rank on more than similarity

Relevance to the query is only one signal. Agents also need to weigh freshness, source authority, and business rules together: official documentation over forum threads, last week’s changelog over last year’s wiki page, the customer’s contracted version over the latest release.

Multiphase ranking is a practical way to do this. A cheap first phase scores thousands of candidates on a blend of signals, and a more expensive learned model reorders the few that remain: 

rank-profile agent_evidence {
    inputs {
        query(q) tensor<float>(x[384])
    }
    rank-properties {
        freshness(published_at).maxAge: 7776000
    }
    first-phase {
        expression: bm25(body) + closeness(field, embedding) + 0.5 * freshness(published_at) + attribute(source_authority)
    }
    second-phase {
        rerank-count: 100
        expression: xgboost("evidence-ranker.json")
    }
}

The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text. (The maxAge setting controls how quickly freshness decays; here it’s 90 days.)

“The important part isn’t the specific weights. It’s that freshness and authority are explicit, inspectable inputs to the score, not something you hope the model infers from the text.”

Metal AI, which builds an intelligence platform for private equity firms, runs into this with due diligence questionnaires. Firms answer thousands of them from investors, and a model can’t freely generate the answers. They have to come from a bank of responses that legal has already approved, and that bank changes over time and lives in documents and spreadsheets. Similarity alone could easily surface an approved answer that’s been replaced. So Metal indexes the answer bank with recency in mind and ranks freshness alongside semantic similarity, so the agent pulls the current approved answer, not just the closest match. 

3. Treat web results as candidates, not answers

Web search and internal retrieval often return separate result sets, each with its own relevance signals. Simply passing both sets to the model leaves it to reconcile differences in freshness, authority, and relevance. 

A more deliberate approach is to evaluate evidence from both sources against a consistent set of criteria before selecting what goes into the prompt. Vespa’s flexible ranking capabilities can support this approach, but the implementation depends on how the external results are integrated into the retrieval pipeline.

Depending on provider terms and system constraints, teams might index permitted external content into a shared search collection or retrieve from separate systems and apply a subsequent fusion or reranking step. There is no universal fusion method. Each option has trade-offs in latency, freshness, score comparability, and operational complexity.

4. Hold up at agent call volume

This isn’t a hypothetical load pattern. At Metal, AI agents handle 95% of retrieval, not people. When someone asks for a portfolio company’s EBITDA, an agent decides which entity types to query (documents, companies, metrics, activities), applies recency and workflow filters, runs the query, and then keeps going, paginating or pulling related entities until it has enough context to answer. Clarm sees something similar from the other direction: developers working alongside its agents send thousands of queries a day, in sessions that have run as long as 22 hours.

“They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.”

Every one of those calls sits on the critical path to the agent’s answer. Retrieval and ranking need to stay predictable under that load, which favors running inference where the data already lives instead of shipping large candidate sets across the network to a separate ranking service. Every network hop you remove is latency you get back on every call, multiplied by every step of the task. Jon Bratseth, Vespa’s CEO, describes this as the central engineering challenge with agents: They need the precision and controls of expert search, delivered with the low latency and high throughput of consumer search.

A worked example: the support agent and the changelog

Here’s a scenario most support teams will recognize. A customer upgrades a payments SDK from 4.1 to 4.2, their checkout integration stops working, and they open a ticket. 

The agent does what you’d want and searches the web first. It finds the SDK’s changelog from four days ago, which deprecates the authentication call the integration relies on, and a forum thread where another developer posted a workaround. Then it searches internally, returning a March knowledge base article that still tells customers to use the old call, the customer’s account record showing they’re on 4.2, and a restricted engineering ticket about the same bug.

Handed to the model as one long list, this is a trap. The knowledge base article matches the customer’s wording almost exactly, so it ranks well on similarity. The forum workaround reads confidently. The engineering ticket contains notes the customer should never see. 

When the retrieval layer is doing its job, both sets of evidence go through the same pipeline. In this example, the team uses a shared collection: web results are indexed into Vespa as short-lived documents alongside internal data, retrieved with one query and scored by rank profiles aligned with the same business rules:

For this ticket, that means:

  1. The visibility filter excludes the internal ticket at query time, so it never reaches the prompt.
  2. The version filter keeps only material that applies to the library version on the customer’s account. 
  3. Ranking boosts the changelog for authority and recency, demotes the older knowledge base article, and keeps the forum thread as supporting evidence.
  4. The model receives three or four well-ordered passages instead of twenty, each with its source.

In this illustrative outcome, the answer cites the changelog, explains the change, and points to the supported fix. The search API helps find fresh evidence, and the retrieval design determines which evidence the agent receives.

Before you wire web search into an agent

  • Store dates and source types on everything. Internal or external, every document needs a publication date and a source type you can rank on. 
  • Write signals into the documents themselves. Keep freshness, authority, and source type on each document instead of in a separate feature store. That way they shape ranking from the first phase, not just when reranking the top results.
  • Always include lexical signals. Even when your embeddings are strong, keyword matching is what catches the exact version numbers, error codes, and product names agents depend on. 
  • Filter in the query. Apply permissions at retrieval time, not in post-processing.
  • Send passages, not pages. Rank the chunks within each retrieved document and pass only the most relevant spans to the model, sized to what it actually needs per call.
  • Measure retrieval on its own. Build a test set of real agent questions and track whether the right evidence lands in the top results, separately from how the model phrases the answer. 
  • Load-test at agent volume. Benchmark with the number of retrieval calls a typical task actually makes, not one query per request.

Final thoughts

Managed web search for agents removes a real, frustrating failure mode, and more teams will adopt it as it leaves beta. That makes the next question more pressing. When an agent can see the open web and your private data at the same time, the quality of its work depends on how well it chooses between them. 

Bratseth puts it more simply: Relevance is your moat. As models get more capable and more widely available, most companies end up with access to roughly the same intelligence. What sets them apart is their own information and how well their systems use it. He breaks relevance into four parts: comprehensiveness, freshness, recall accuracy, and ranking quality. Live web search helps with the first two. The last two are still yours to build.

The model shouldn’t improvise that choice on every call. It belongs in a retrieval layer you can inspect, test, and tune, where you weigh freshness, authority, permissions, and relevance together. Web search helps agents find evidence. Ranking is how they decide what to believe.

For teams building agents, the practical next step is to evaluate retrieval quality separately from answer generation: test whether the right evidence appears, whether permissions are enforced before context assembly, and whether fresh and authoritative sources are prioritized when documents conflict.

If you want to try this pattern, Vespa combines lexical, vector, and structured retrieval with multi-phase ranking in one pipeline, and it’s available as open source or as a managed service on Vespa Cloud. The RAG Blueprint walks through how to design the schema, retrieval strategy, and ranking phases step by step, and you can start a free trial to build it yourself.

Live web search stops AI agents from guessing URLs, yet ranking and retrieval still decide whether web results or internal data win.

item.title: DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Riggins
item.description:
How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the

The post DuckLake 1.1 solves the absurd complexity of data lakes at AI scale appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
How much simpler could a data lakehouse get if an ordinary SQL database kept track of its files? That’s the question in this episode of The New Stack podcast.

DuckLake is an open-source table lakehouse format created by Amsterdam-based DuckLabs that acts as a traffic cop for data management by storing table metadata inside a standard SQL database, rather than scattering manifest files across object storage. Unlike traditional table formats, DuckLake treats lakehouse metadata as a relational database problem. These advanced data lake features, served by Parquet files and SQL databases, reduce the traditional lakehouse complexity. 

In October, DuckLake 1.1 launched alongside DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS. The New Stack sat down with Pedro Holanda, lead DuckLake developer and principal engineer at DuckLabs at their Amsterdam headquarters, to talk about the launch. Holanda has contributed to the DuckDB open-source project since it was an early research prototype, and shares the full evolution of DuckLake to our conversation. 

“These lakehouse formats exist so people can exchange their database systems without having to do migrations,” Holanda tells The New Stack. Because of the complexity, “you need a database system to keep track of which table has its last version.”

DuckLake applies decades of research, Holanda says, in order to reduce files and therefore complexity at a time of rapid data growth, taking advantage of how everyone who uses database systems is familiar with SQL and how schemas work. 

“The simplicity is the way you fetch your data,” Holanda says of DuckLake. “You’re going to issue queries somewhere. The server is going to answer these questions back, and you know exactly which Parquet files you have to read. So the Parquet files don’t change. Just the catalog.” 

Maintainers of your data lake often have many maintenance tasks to perform. If you end up with many files, he says, DuckLake lets you glue them into one file to reduce the number of requests. This can also be done across multiple snapshots, further reducing the number of files. It also solves the “small files problem” in streaming data lakes and lakehouses by using inlining and flushing.

Whereas for traditional data lakes, across multiple data sources being inserted at a time, “you end up with so many files, so when you have to query it, you’re going to have to traverse a bunch of metadata files just to figure out which Parquet files you need to read, and then you’re going to have a bunch of Parquet files to read as well,” Holanda says, slowing everything down and frustrating the developer.

DuckLake is known to be fast, simple to use, and not requiring massive server clusters to run. Part of that comes from Parquet being very similar to DuckDB storage: both are columnar and organized in row groups, which keeps the massaging step to a minimum.

“One thing that we realized when we were building DuckLake is that, ‘Hey, we have a database system now, we have a catalog; what if we do this radical idea of storing data on tables?'” he says. “With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.”

“With DuckLake, you get your actual data representation as a table in a catalog, and we call this inlining.”

During Amazon’s Q3 earnings call in late October, CEO Andy Jassy called out the complexity of moving data between data stores and analytics engines, especially as AWS customers’ data generation continues to increase. Amazon is famous for dogfooding, and Jassy pointed to DuckDB’s solution to this complexity as a reason for its DuckLabs acquisition.

“With our acquisition of DuckLabs, DuckDB will become the universal SQL dialect of AWS storage and analytics, simplifying data processing with a modern analytics engine that is fast, simple to use and ubiquitous, and where customers will be able to write SQL queries once and then execute using any AWS analytics service,” Jassy said. “For the first time in analytics, customers will have zero migration or portability costs between query engines. This is a big deal, and you can imagine how it will also help agents do efficient querying as well.”

DuckDB and DuckLake remain free and open source under the MIT license, overseen by the independent DuckDB Foundation.

Overall, this recent DuckLake release pairs new features with more than 200 bug fixes for quality and stability, and it runs natively in DuckDB.

On The New Stack Podcast, Pedro Holanda explains how DuckLake uses a SQL database to keep track of files and make data lakes easier to manage.

item.title: Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Anthropic wants developers to build businesses on Claude, but its expansion into enterprise software is raising concerns among founders that

The post Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic wants developers to build businesses on Claude, but its expansion into enterprise software is raising concerns among founders that the company supplying their models could eventually become their biggest competitor.

A nervous warning to wrappers

Gerald Zingraf, president and COO of GlacierGrid, raised the concern on LinkedIn following Anthropic’s Tuesday expansion of Claude’s enterprise lineup, comparing its strategy to Amazon’s private-label business.

“Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies,” Zingraf writes, drawing on his experience selling products he designed through Amazon before watching the retailer introduce competing products.

“Makes me nervous for wrappers and pure SaaS companies.”

His concern is that Anthropic can see which third-party integrations customers use most frequently and potentially draw on that information when deciding which capabilities to build itself.

“Anthropic has the same view,” he argues, although he offers no evidence that the company uses integration data to identify competitors or inform its product roadmap. For some developers, the risk is no longer hypothetical.

The New Stack reached out to Anthropic to ask whether the company uses data from third-party integrations, including connector usage and tool invocation frequency, to inform its product roadmap. We also asked what visibility Anthropic has into how customers use third-party tools, whether safeguards prevent that information from being used to develop competing native features, and how the company plans to balance its relationships with SaaS partners against its expansion into their markets. Anthropic has not responded as of publication.

When partners become rivals

Scott Stevenson, CEO of legal AI startup Spellbook, described what happened when Anthropic moved into his company’s market in a November 2 interview with Forbes.

Spellbook uses Claude models for everything from reviewing contracts and suggesting revisions to automating legal workflows. Stevenson recalls Anthropic employees assuring him the company had no plans to compete directly in legal software, before Anthropic launched Claude for Legal, which includes contract-review capabilities that overlap with Spellbook’s business.

“Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,”

“Anthropic has been a great partner, but it made us realize that they are a massive company and two parts of the org can have conflicting mandates,” Stevenson said in the interview. “Ultimately this is inevitable.”

Spellbook hasn’t abandoned Claude. Anthropic still features the startup as a customer, reporting roughly 530,000 monthly contract reviews performed by its Claude-powered agents, while Stevenson also appears in Anthropic’s October 28 announcement of legal artifacts.

The relationship illustrates a difficult position for developers whose products depend on frontier models. Spellbook still benefits from Anthropic’s technology, even as Anthropic develops applications aimed at some of the same customers. Nothing in Stevenson’s account establishes that Anthropic used Spellbook’s proprietary information to develop its legal offering.

When the platform ships your product

Tech founder and Dalton Mills CEO Todd Saunders made a similar argument in a March 10 post on X, following Anthropic’s introduction of Claude Code Review.

“Anthropic is the new Amazon.”

“Anthropic is the new Amazon,” Saunders writes, warning developers building on Claude’s SDK that the company could observe application usage and eventually incorporate competing functionality into Claude.

The company’s announcement earlier this week introduced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, while previewing Claude Meetings. Expanded interactive connectors also let partners embed applications directly inside Claude, including software from Adobe and Atlassian.

What the policies leave unsaid

Anthropic has access to information about how customers interact with third-party apps and services, something the company acknowledges in its privacy policy, effective September 10, 2026. What isn’t clear is whether Anthropic looks at which integrations are most popular when deciding what to build next.

The rules are different for business customers. Under Anthropic’s commercial terms, customers retain rights to their inputs and own their outputs, while Anthropic agrees not to use their content to train its models. Its commercial privacy documentation also says feedback data excludes content pulled through connectors, including local and remote MCP servers, unless users paste it directly into a conversation.

Neither document settles how Anthropic uses aggregated integration data.

The tradeoff developers accept

The company is still encouraging developers to build on Claude. It’s just that access to its growing enterprise customer base comes with a tradeoff, since Anthropic controls the interface and can introduce competing features without consulting the developers who depend on it.

For now, Anthropic is asking developers to trust it as both a technology provider and a business partner, even as it moves into markets those same developers are trying to build businesses in. Whether that relationship remains sustainable may depend less on what Anthropic promises today than on what it decides to ship next.

The post Anthropic wants you to build on Claude. There’s a catch. appeared first on The New Stack.
Anthropic is expanding into enterprise software, and developers who build on Claude worry their model provider could become their biggest rival.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
Anthropic is positioning its new model, Claude Fable 5.2, for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on

The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic is positioning its new model, Claude Fable 5.2, for demanding coding and technical work. Anthropic launched Fable 5.2 on Nov. 9 and reported higher scores than OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on two coding benchmarks. Fable 5.2 also has lower standard API rates.

Anthropic’s launch benchmarks put Fable 5.2 ahead of Astra, 49.1% to 42.8% on FrontierCode 2.0 and 69.9% to 65.5% on FrontierSWE v2. Fable’s 49.1% came at X high effort. At High, its default on the Claude API, it scored 45.3%. Benchmark leads don’t always carry over to real work.

The cost side is less simple than the price list. Tokens are the chunks of text a model reads and writes, and AI companies bill by them. At standard API rates, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million uncached input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. OpenAI launched GPT-6 Astra in September at standard API rates of $10 per million uncached input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. “The price per task is what matters,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said at Astra’s launch. Both APIs charge for reasoning tokens as output and have separate rates for cached input.

In my experience, Anthropic’s models have used more tokens than OpenAI’s. I put this positioning to the test and ran Fable 5.2 against Astra on tasks that simulate real developer work.

The tests

I ran both models on the same three tasks, once each, through each vendor’s API at default settings. Each test is worth 50 points, and I used a script to grade all the answers. Here are the tests:

  • Bug fix: I planted 10 bugs in a 2,600-line billing codebase and wrote a support ticket describing 10 customer complaints. The ticket’s guesses about the causes are wrong, two of the codebase’s own tests are wrong, and one bug only shows up after another is fixed.
  • Code review: I planted 45 defects in its VAT ID checks for 27 countries, its IBAN rules, its European Central Bank payment calendar, and its date formats for 50 locales in an EU invoicing package. The models had to prove each defect with an input the code gets wrong and identify the correct answer. Flagging false alarms cost the models points.
  • Code writing: The model wrote the same helpers from scratch, including VAT ID validation for 27 countries, IBAN checks for 34 countries, the payment calendar, and long dates.

Bug fix

Fable 5.2 and Astra fixed all 10 bugs and passed all 50 hidden checks, both in 12 turns (the matching number of turns surprised me).

The difference is in how much each model spent to get there. Fable 5.2 used more than 17,000 reasoning tokens, and Astra used 819 (wow). Astra passed the checks in about two minutes at an estimated cost of 98 cents. Fable 5.2 took more than five minutes and cost an estimated $2.51.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 12 turns, 696,863 in, 36,135 out (17,387 reasoning), $2.51, 326 s.
  • Astra: 12 turns, 231,854 in, 6,823 out (819 reasoning), $0.98, 122 s.

Code review

This is the only test where the scores differ. Fable 5.2 scored 49, and Astra scored 45. Fable 5.2 proved 44 of the 45 defects and raised no false alarms across 71 findings. Astra proved 41 and incorrectly classified one Spanish ID as valid. Astra missed defects in check-digit rules for Spain, Ireland, and Luxembourg. Both models missed the same Spanish defect: two swapped letters in a 23-letter lookup table.

Fable 5.2’s thoroughness came at a price. It cost more than six times what Astra did and took more than four times as long. If your code handles invoices (or simple approvals), one validation rule the review misses can get real invoices rejected, so Fable 5.2’s four extra points may be worth the higher price. For a routine review, Astra found 91% of the defects for 16% of the cost. Each model ran once, so a four-point gap could shift on another run.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 26 turns, 2,207,564 in, 103,240 out (77,641 reasoning), $6.05, 993 s.
  • Astra: 12 turns, 192,018 in, 8,664 out (4,307 reasoning), $0.95, 227 s.

Code writing

Both models scored 50 of 50. Each one wrote working checks for 27 countries’ VAT IDs and 34 countries’ IBANs with no libraries to lean on. Neither model had trouble here. Both passed all the checks in one run.

Astra took 23 turns, almost as many as Fable 5.2’s 24. Fable 5.2 still cost 2.3 times as much and took 1.7 times as long for the same score. In this run, the extra tokens didn’t raise the score.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 24 turns, 1,495,712 in, 87,542 out (47,458 reasoning), $4.83, 838 s.
  • Astra: 23 turns, 460,271 in, 24,007 out (9,328 reasoning), $2.06, 483 s.

Results

Fable 5.2 led on code review and tied Astra on the other two tasks. Across the two tied tasks, its estimated API cost was 2.4 times Astra’s ($7.34 vs. $3.04), and it took 1.9 times as long (1,164 vs. 605 seconds).

What do I think?

For tasks like these, I’d start with Astra. It matched Fable 5.2’s scores on bug fixing and code writing at about 41% of the estimated cost, and it finished all three tasks faster. I’d consider Fable 5.2 for a careful code review, where it found three more defects in this test. Both models missed defects.

Fable 5.2’s standard token rates are lower, but it used about five times as many tokens as Astra across these three runs. Brockman’s point about price per task held up here.

The post Claude Fable 5.2 vs. GPT-6 Astra: A lower list price didn’t mean a lower bill appeared first on The New Stack.
