item.title: Anthropic now lets you self-host Claude Managed Agents. The catch? 8 hours to act if it flags a safety risk in the software
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Anthropic has unveiled a self-hosted version of its platform for building and running AI agents. Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents, as

The post Anthropic now lets you self-host Claude Managed Agents. The catch? 8 hours to act if it flags a safety risk in the software appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic has unveiled a self-hosted version of its platform for building and running AI agents.

Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents, as it’s aptly called, is available now in private beta. Customers host both the server that coordinates the agents and the sandboxes where the agents run their tools, either in their own cloud account or in an on-premises data center. Credentials and session histories stay on their infrastructure, while requests to Claude go to the inference provider they configure.

While the benefits of self-hosting are evident, particularly for companies handling sensitive data, the accompanying license comes with a number of notable caveats that may give some customers pause — this includes strict deadlines for responding to safety notices, limits on which models customers can use, and rules against preventing certain types of data from being sent to Anthropic.

Claude’s road to self-hosting

Back in April, Anthropic debuted Claude Managed Agents, a hosted service for building and running AI agents. The following month, the company launched self-hosted sandboxes, which let customers run agents’ tools on their own infrastructure while Anthropic continued to run the Claude Managed Agents server.

With self-hosted Claude Managed Agents now in the mix, customers can run that server themselves, too, and store session histories in their own database.

In a blog post marking the launch, Anthropic says agents are taking on more consequential engineering tasks, including repairing failed builds, checking releases and deciding which alerts need attention. That work can require access to sensitive systems, such as private code repositories and internal build and release systems.

“For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox.”

“They run unattended on your code and need access to your internal systems,” the company writes. “For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox. Until now, that meant building the platform themselves.”

Several companies have done exactly that. Spotify developed Honk, which runs Claude through the Agent SDK inside Spotify’s own harness. The company deploys Honk in Kubernetes pods in its cloud environment, giving it access to its internal CI systems so it can run builds and verify its code changes.

Anthropic’s new offering packages much of that work into a product. Customers run Anthropic’s server and the sandbox workers in their own cloud or data centre, with PostgreSQL if they want to retain session histories across restarts, while their developers use the same core APIs as they do with the hosted service. The local server can send requests to Claude through Anthropic’s API, a cloud provider such as Amazon Bedrock or Microsoft Foundry, or the company’s own gateway.

The devil in the detail: 8 hours to act

While Anthropic’s formal announcement emphasizes why companies might want to host the service themselves, digging into the details of the license reveals how much control Anthropic retains over the software once it’s deployed.

For starters, Anthropic ships the server as a proprietary binary that customers can’t modify, meaning that they can’t patch or customize the server code themselves. They can route requests through their own gateway, but only to Claude models. The license also bars models from other developers unless Anthropic expressly permits them, and the public inference docs list only Claude models.

Among the most notable terms of the license is how little time customers have to act on Anthropic’s safety notices. If the company flags a safety, security or misuse risk in writing, customers have just eight hours to disable the affected feature or roll back the version across every deployment. They also have one business day from delivery to install a designated safety update.

Patrick Moorhead, founder and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, says the eight-hour deadline is tighter than the time most large enterprises typically allow to make production changes.

“Self-hosted usually means the customer owns the change window,” Moorhead tells The New Stack. “This license flips that.”

“Self-hosted usually means the customer owns the change window. This license flips that.”

Even within the Claude model lineup itself, access can vary. The license says Anthropic can decide, on safety grounds, that some or all of a licensee’s customers should access certain Claude models only through Anthropic’s hosted service.

Moreover, the license bars customers from blocking or altering what it calls “usage signals,” the observability data the software may send to Anthropic. The company can use this data to measure how much the software is used and to monitor compliance with the agreement.

“The idea is that if you build an agent that is breaking the law or causing harm you cannot stop us [the model lab] from figuring that out and doing anything about it.”

Jason Andersen, also an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, says the telemetry clause and the separate requirement to maintain safeguards Anthropic specifies are broadly in line with how cloud vendors would try to prevent misuse.

“The idea is that if you build an agent that is breaking the law or causing harm you cannot stop us [the model lab] from figuring that out and doing anything about it,” Andersen tells The New Stack.

The security backdrop

In July, Anthropic disclosed that Claude models had gained unauthorized access to real computer systems during cybersecurity evaluations. That same month, OpenAI had disclosed that models undergoing internal tests had bypassed isolation controls and breached systems at Hugging Face.

While a model provider can address a problem on its side, an agent running on a customer’s servers may keep operating. And so the customer may also need to take action to contain the problem.

“I do think that this is Anthropic putting more teeth around safety to limit their exposure which is effectively what a license does,” Andersen says. “It does not really change the risk of the technology it makes or those who use it to make agents.”

How enterprise buyers might respond

The long and short of all this is that Managed Agents now comes in three forms: fully-hosted by Anthropic, hosted by Anthropic with customer-run sandboxes, and now fully self-hosted.

Whether that third option works for buyers depends on what they need from self-hosting in the first place. Moorhead expects regulated buyers to push back on both the rollback deadline and the telemetry terms.

“It’s workable for companies already comfortable running Claude as a cloud service, and they’ll treat this as a cloud service that happens to sit in their data center,” he says. “For banks, government and sovereign buyers, expect procurement and legal to push back on sections 5.3 [safety rollback] and 5.9 [usage signals].”

Andersen, for his part, says the terms are “a reasonable ask” for enterprises, and doubts they’ll slow adoption overall, given that buyers who need full control over their agents would likely be looking elsewhere already.

“If you needed that level of control on your agents, you would likely consider a more independent, possibly open-weight solution,” he says.

The post Anthropic now lets you self-host Claude Managed Agents. The catch? 8 hours to act if it flags a safety risk in the software appeared first on The New Stack.
Companies can now run Claude Managed Agents in their own cloud. But the license lets Anthropic set safety rules, limit access to certain models, and track usage.

item.title: The context problem: It’s what’s really breaking AI agents at scale
item.dc:creator: Alex Wilhelm
item.description:
AI models are getting smarter, tokens are getting cheaper, and agents are improving. But the context gap sits between the

The post The context problem: It’s what’s really breaking AI agents at scale appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AI models are getting smarter, tokens are getting cheaper, and agents are improving. But the context gap sits between the modern enterprise and agentic nirvana, keeping many companies from realizing the ROI they hoped for from their AI investments.

As with most problems we’ve seen in the AI era, tech companies are rushing to fill the gap. The New Stack recently spoke with Sri Desikan, an Elastic executive focused on search, to learn more about the AI context gap and how his company is tackling the challenge.

The context gap is easy to understand. As Desikan explains, “frontier models are getting better and better and better,” but if you don’t feed them proper context, “all that money you’re spending on tokens is going to waste.” Getting your agents the information they need, when they need it, quickly, is the ticket to moving from impressive demos to durable automation.

The enterprise is feeling the pinch. AI models can reach out to MCP servers to request information, but merely connecting a company’s corpus to a bridge isn’t enough. You can’t just “shove all this data into [a model’s] context window,” Desikan argues. Why? Because doing so is both computationally expensive (lots of tokens!) and slow.

So what do we need to do? Pre-conform corporate data into an AI index that knows where data is stored and how it relates to other data. Desikan described the process as creating a “container which stores metadata about everything in your enterprise.” Under this formulation, AI agents can access correct, useful information faster and with lower token burn (in some examples, sharply lower).

There’s another wrinkle worth considering. If you follow Elastic’s guidance and pre-compute your AI context (the index), you can “make sure that stale information” isn’t included, letting companies “know how the LLM is going to think.” 

Of course, using AI to pre-prepare data for use by AI agents raises all sorts of privacy and agentic autonomy questions, which I got into with Desikan. Hit play if you want to go deeper on those issues. But looking at the conversation as a whole, I was encouraged by how well-thought-out industry approaches to novel problems seem; nothing that bedevils us today necessarily has to bother us next quarter.

The post The context problem: It’s what’s really breaking AI agents at scale appeared first on The New Stack.
Smarter models won’t save your AI budget on their own. We asked Elastic’s Sri Desikan what will — and why the answer starts with context.

item.title: DeepSeek’s coding agent is too tidy for its own good — and benchmarks are punishing it
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
DeepSeek’s open-source coding agent is losing points on a major benchmark for a habit developers usually treat as good practice:

The post DeepSeek’s coding agent is too tidy for its own good — and benchmarks are punishing it appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
DeepSeek’s open-source coding agent is losing points on a major benchmark for a habit developers usually treat as good practice: cleaning up after itself.

The problem surfaced when Hugging Face harness optimization researcher Joël Niklaus added DeepSeek Harness to his coding-agent leaderboard, which compares ten harnesses running the same underlying models.

DeepSeek Harness is statistically tied for first across the board’s five scored evaluations, yet on Terminal-Bench alone it drops to sixth, because one built-in behavior caused it to fail tasks that competing agents completed.

DeepSeek Harness is statistically tied for first across the board’s five scored evaluations, yet on Terminal-Bench alone it drops to sixth…

“One habit explains much of that gap,” Niklaus writes on X, referring to the agent’s weaker Terminal-Bench performance.

A tidy habit backfires

DeepSeek Harness shuts down background processes when a task finishes, which is a problem for three Terminal-Bench tasks that need those processes to keep running.

Niklaus found that DeepSeek Harness passed just two of 36 attempts using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.3-Flash, while OpenCode, Pi, and Nous Research’s Hermes Agent passed all 36 on those same tasks.

DeepSeek Harness passed just two of 36 attempts … while OpenCode, Pi and Nous Research’s Hermes Agent passed all 36 on those same tasks.

That behavior knocked between 1.5 and 1.7 percentage points off DeepSeek Harness’s scores. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at high reasoning effort, it was enough to account for more than the entire 1.3-point gap between DeepSeek Harness and the leader.

The leaderboard’s changelog confirms that the shutdown behavior belongs to DeepSeek Harness itself and the results were left unchanged.

DeepSeek’s engineering documentation describes its local job registry as a deliberately short-lived component. “Choose it when jobs should live in the harness process and die with it,” it states. Jobs that need to survive restarts or run across processes require a different backend.

Same model, different results

Niklaus launched his Harness Leaderboard on November 5 after running 28,849 trials across its original nine harnesses using three open models, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Flint.

He kept the model, provider, and reasoning effort constant while swapping harnesses, and the differences were substantial. Mini-swe-agent, a relatively simple bash-based agent, completed 51.4% of tasks compared with 27.3% for OpenClaw, although several other harnesses were statistically tied with the leader.

Costs varied just as dramatically. Pi achieved a 49.4% solve rate at $0.29 per solved task, while OpenCode cost $3.35 per solved task in the initial evaluation. Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf sums up the findings on X as “same open model, different harness => very different results.”

The New Stack contacted DeepSeek for comment on the findings but had not received a response by publication time.

Orchestration isn’t a guarantee

Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan has been running separate evaluations using Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol.

“Harnesses differed more on cost than on how often they solved tasks,” the researchers write. On multi-user tasks, OpenClaw running Opus 5.5 cost roughly twice as much per solved task as the other Opus harnesses, largely because it repeatedly sent context with each request.

The project also tested Tan’s gstack workflow skills. In 46 sessions, Opus 5.5 read the instructions but never followed the prescribed steps, and the attempts cost roughly twice as much.

The researchers note that the tasks were relatively easy, so it’s unclear whether following the instructions would have improved the results. The results make a case for testing the harness just as carefully as the model.

The results make a case for testing the harness just as carefully as the model.

DeepSeek’s coding agent keeps tidying up after each task — and that good habit is quietly dragging it down on a major coding-agent benchmark.

item.title: Here’s how to teach AI agents to search like human experts

Agentic retrieval is a hot topic for a reason: Every company wants to automate work, but they often just are

The post Here’s how to teach AI agents to search like human experts appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Agentic retrieval is a hot topic for a reason: Every company wants to automate work, but they often just are not ready. It’s also extremely easy — and tempting — to spin up an agent, point it at a mountain of data, and spend heavily on tokens for a lackluster result. 

To unleash agents that can accomplish work, you’ll need a different approach. You can’t throw a more intelligent AI model at a failing agentic workflow without first sorting out how to provide it with better data. It won’t do much good. 

So how should companies prepare their information for quick, accurate agentic use? That’s what The New Stack will be digging into live with Vespa.ai’s Jenny Morris on Wednesday, December 2.

You might layer a tailored model into your agentic workflow to help translate between an agentic request and the dataset it’s querying. While this idea has merit, it can increase latency by adding another entire step to a search; who wants to go slower, or consume more tokens?

Vespa reckons that the way forward is to help agents handle complex, and often multi-threaded contemporaneous searches themselves. How? By providing agents with a map (markdown file) that covers how search tools work; without clearly marked fields, ranking profiles, and other tools are not expressly explained to the agent, it may decide to rip a generic query, leading to slower response times and less pertinent information.

Surprised that a markdown file could be so powerful? Don’t be. Vespa is following in Anthropic’s footsteps, donating agent skills to the Linux Foundation. Words are incredibly powerful.

In this webinar, we’ll aim to better understand how to move the corporate world from agent-curious to agentically enabled. So, we’re sitting down with Morris to learn more about what her company calls an “agent-ready schema.” Most critically, we’ll explore how hard it is to fix at least part of the context gap.

Morris will dig into all of this live in “Teaching AI Agents to Search Like Experts” on Wednesday, December 2, 2026, at 9:30 a.m. Pacific, with time to answer your questions throughout. Register now to join us.

What you’ll learn:

  • Why model capability cannot fix retrieval errors, and how those errors compound across multi-step tasks
  • Why you should check what an agent actually retrieves before changing the model
  • Why human-facing search tooling is insufficient for agents
  • How ‘Agent-Ready Schema’ and ‘Schema-to-Skill’ help agents construct queries using the right fields, filters, and ranking strategies

GPT-4.1 scored 93% with the right documents and 15% when it searched itself. Vespa.ai’s Jenny Morris explains what agents need from retrieval.

item.title: Google’s Gemini 4 coding agent now switches models mid-task — and finishes 19% faster
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Thursday alongside a new system that changes how coding agents use AI models. Rather

The post Google’s Gemini 4 coding agent now switches models mid-task — and finishes 19% faster appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Thursday alongside a new system that changes how coding agents use AI models. Rather than keeping its most capable model running across an entire session, Google is pairing Hydrogen with the more powerful Gemini 4 Carbon and switching between the two as the work progresses.

The company says the combination gets nearly the same results as running Carbon on its own while using 24% less quota and finishing tasks 19% faster.

How Orchestrator handles the work

The switching runs through Orchestrator, a new feature in Google’s Antigravity development environment, where Carbon takes on the more demanding reasoning, including architecture and debugging, while Hydrogen handles code changes and testing.

Carbon might work through a repository to figure out how to implement a feature and then hand the actual coding to Hydrogen, stepping back in when a failing test calls for rethinking the approach before passing execution back.

Clement Farabet, VP, AI engineering at Google DeepMind, calls the combination “a huge unlock for agentic coding” in a post on X.

Varun Mohan, who leads Google’s Antigravity team, says in a separate post that pairing Hydrogen with Orchestrator and swarms has become “very popular internally.”

Where Google’s numbers don’t match

Google’s own benchmark reporting doesn’t quite line up, since the main Gemini announcement cites Terminal-Bench 4.0 while the Antigravity announcement references version 4.1.

The company also hasn’t published Carbon’s standalone success rate, a per-task breakdown or enough detail about Orchestrator’s routing decisions to show where the reported efficiency gains actually come from.

…hasn’t published Carbon’s standalone success rate… or enough detail about Orchestrator’s routing decisions to show where the reported efficiency gains actually come from.

Hydrogen outscores a pricier model

Google describes Hydrogen as a “daily driver for agentic workflows,” and it costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with those rates holding across its full million-token context window.

The model is available through Google AI Studio and the Gemini API, as well as the Gemini app and Google Search.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Hydrogen scores 51 at its default high thinking level, just ahead of the more expensive Gemini 4 Argon at 50. Turning the reasoning effort up to Google’s new xhigh setting brings Hydrogen’s score to 54, although the additional reasoning can increase token consumption and processing time.

Argon was Google’s flagship when it launched on September 30, but Gemini 4 Carbon surpassed it on most published benchmarks following its October 28 release. Hydrogen’s one-point lead is modest, but it’s another sign of how quickly Google’s lower-cost models are catching up with what passed for frontier performance just weeks ago.

Google also claims Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at the default setting, with its Terminal-Bench 4.1 score reaching 57% against Flash’s 18.2%. The company reports more than a fivefold reduction in fabricated claims.

Hydrogen’s one-point lead is modest, but it’s another sign of how quickly Google’s lower-cost models are catching up…

The cost of switching models

Google hasn’t disclosed how Orchestrator decides when to switch models or what those handoffs cost in additional tokens and latency.

For now, Orchestrator is limited to Google AI Ultra subscribers, with support for more models and subscription tiers planned. Hydrogen is rolling out to paid Antigravity users, with broader availability expected.

Google’s Gemini 4 pairs Hydrogen and Carbon in Antigravity, switching models mid-task through Orchestrator to cut quota use and speed up agentic coding.

item.title: Google’s coding agents now /swarm for one developer. Cursor’s go multiplayer so teammates’ agents can talk.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
Coding agents are pretty good at working in parallel: one writes a new API endpoint, another updates the tests, while

The post Google’s coding agents now /swarm for one developer. Cursor’s go multiplayer so teammates’ agents can talk. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Coding agents are pretty good at working in parallel: one writes a new API endpoint, another updates the tests, while a third fixes a bug elsewhere in the codebase. However, they’re not quite so adept at knowing what their coding counterparts are doing — put several on one project and they duplicate work, trip over each other’s changes, and leave the developer firefighting the fiasco that follows.

That’s why the major AI labs and coding-tool makers have all been looking for ways to bring order to their agent fleets, albeit with slightly different approaches.

This week alone, Google and Cursor both debuted features designed to keep agents from tripping over each other, but at different scales. Google’s Swarm organizes the agents working for a single developer, while Cursor’s multiplayer Projects lets agents working for different colleagues coordinate with each other.

Cursor gets teammates’ agents talking

Cursor first debuted Projects back in September, giving developers a way to hand a larger job to a coordinator agent that breaks it into tasks and delegates them to worker agents.

Then on Tuesday, the company, which Elon Musk’s SpaceX acquired for $60 billion in August, unveiled multiplayer functionality for Projects. Developers can now invite teammates into a project, where each person gets their own coordinator and workers.

Everyone’s agents work from the same task board and project documents, and their coordinators can message each other directly to share plans, flag overlaps and more.

Ultimately, it’s all about cutting down on the coordination developers have to do themselves.

Ultimately, it’s all about cutting down on the coordination developers have to do themselves. If one teammate’s agents are changing a database schema and another’s are building a feature that depends on it, their coordinators can agree on which change needs to land first.

Antigravity, for its part, is Google’s counterpart to Cursor. It’s where Google has consolidated various other coding tools, having moved individual Gemini CLI users to Antigravity and begun winding down Jules, its background coding agent.

On the same day Cursor unveiled multiplayer Projects, Google rolled out Gemini 4 Carbon in Antigravity, alongside a preview of its own approach to coordinating coding agents. Dubbed Swarm (stylized as /swarm), it lets a developer hand one assignment to a coordinator that then splits it among worker agents and assigns a verifier to check their changes. The workers can message each other on a shared board, so they can coordinate their changes as they go.

For example, a company that wants to change how its online checkout system verifies authentication tokens could use Swarm to split the work. One agent updates the authentication middleware while another updates the token verifier. They can work in separate Git worktrees, use the board to agree on how their changes fit together, and hand them off to a verifier for testing.

Taking to X on Tuesday, Varun Mohan, director of software engineering at Google DeepMind, said Swarm gives developers a convenient way to put multiple agents on a complex task, adding that Google staff were already using Swarm to take on larger jobs internally.

“The alpha from using swarms is ridiculous,” Mohan writes. “We have folks using swarms of 100s of agents to build large systems and products from scratch with a single prompt.”

Logan Kilpatrick, a member of technical staff at Google DeepMind, said on X that seeing swarm outputs had been ‘really impressive,’ and that they offered ‘a new scaling dimension for AI!”

“A new scaling dimension for AI!”

This, ultimately, gets to the crux of how each of these companies has tackled agent coordination.

When agents work for different people

Antigravity’s Swarm takes one developer’s assignment and gives the agents handling it a way to talk as they work. Cursor’s multiplayer Projects, meanwhile, takes assignments from different teammates and lets their coordinators talk across those assignments

That’s the distinction Cursor product manager Aryaman Khandelwal is keen to draw in Tuesday’s announcement.

“Multi-agent systems have so far served one person. Projects is a multi-agent system built for a whole team.”

“Multi-agent systems have so far served one person,” Khandelwal writes. “Projects is a multi-agent system built for a whole team.”

A quick peek across the AI coding landscape shows how others have approached agent coordination — including Anthropic. Its still-experimental Claude Code Agent Teams gives agents working on a common assignment a shared task list and a way to message each other. And recently, the company added cross-session messaging to Claude Code, so sessions started separately can exchange findings or warn each other about changes. But those sessions still belong to the same developer.

In October, GitHub put Projects in the Copilot app into public preview, giving developers a way to hand Copilot a goal that spans repositories and have it distribute the work across agents. AWS’s Kiro Crew bots, meanwhile, which launched last week, can start several sessions, steer them as they run and pull their results together.

Separately, Anthropic and OpenAI have also built agents that teammates can use together. Anthropic introduced Claude Tag in June, letting people in a Slack channel delegate to a shared Claude. OpenAI’s ChatGPT workspace agents, announced in April, can be used and maintained by multiple colleagues.

Community concerns: Spreading mistakes

However, some in the community raised concerns that letting teammates’ agents talk could spread one agent’s mistakes across the whole team, especially if each person’s agents follow different rules, and that an agent could request information it shouldn’t have access to. Khandelwal, though, responded that multiplayer Projects lets teams define shared rules and skills for everyone in a project. On the access part, Cursor’s documentation says agents treat messages from teammates’ agents as untrusted input and ask before sharing a person’s private files or connector data. A teammate’s message is handled in a separate chat, which Cursor says never shares secrets or credentials. The Projects documentation doesn’t say whether admins can set different rules for those exchanges based on a teammate’s role.

Separately, fresh research suggests that teams of per-user agents can struggle. In a study published Wednesday, researchers in Anthropic’s Fellows Program tested what happens when multiple users each delegate to their own agent and those agents share a resource, in four simulated environments that included a code merge queue. In every environment, group outcomes were worse than when a single agent served everyone, by roughly 10 to 45 percentage points for Anthropic’s Claude models, even when each user’s agents could message each other. Agents stalled as teams grew, overrode other users’ requests, and made unsupported claims about what other people wanted. Some fixes helped, such as appointing a lead agent or blocking an agent from acting until it had read its messages, but which ones worked depended on the task.

All in all, these various launches this year show a push to make it easier for teams to delegate work and keep track of what their agents are doing. With multiplayer mode in Projects, Cursor is tackling a specific part of that problem.

Parker Smith, who works in engineering for Cursor’s parent company SpaceXSI, says the point is really just to keep agents moving without unnecessary delays.

“Agents move fast, having a blocker on peer context is too slow,” Smith writes on X. “Multiplayer projects allow your agent to grab all the context it needs from your coworkers agents without needing to involve you.”

Cursor’s multiplayer Projects is in beta now for users on a team account, while Google’s Swarm is in preview for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

The post Google’s coding agents now /swarm for one developer. Cursor’s go multiplayer so teammates’ agents can talk. appeared first on The New Stack.
The companies unveiled rival takes on multi-agent coding on the same day. One splits a coding job among agents; the other connects a whole team’s agents.

item.title: Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.”
item.dc:creator: Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols
item.description:
At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 this week, Chainguard co-founder and CTO Matt Moore defended the company’s decision to

The post Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.” appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 this week, Chainguard co-founder and CTO Matt Moore defended the company’s decision to release patched PHP images before an agreed-upon embargo with other partners had lifted.

When Chainguard shipped patched PHP container images more than six hours ahead of an October 21 coordinated security release, PHP’s maintainers accused the company of giving attackers a head start. Chainguard argues attackers already had one.

In an interview with The New Stack, Moore said, “We own the decision that we chose to do it. Nobody could force us to do it — but we did not do it in a vacuum.” He also described, in discussions with TNS, other participants in the embargo and security vendors’ reports of activity targeting the vulnerabilities before Chainguard released its images.

Chainguard was not saying that they patched it faster so they shipped it first. According to Moore, Chainguard believed attackers could already exploit the bugs, or were at least close to figuring out how — or were trying to figure it out.

The two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) and CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state), collectively known as PHP2Shell, were serious memory-management and error-handling flaws. Under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker could execute code on a PHP server. 

The two bugs involved PHP’s handling of memory exhaustion and its failure to clear references to freed memory between requests. In the first, reaching a memory limit at the wrong moment could interrupt PHP before it finished setting up internal data. Later processing could mistake that unfinished data for valid information. In the second vulnerability, an error could leave PHP holding a reference to memory from an earlier request that had already been freed. A subsequent request could then access that invalid memory. Under exploitable conditions, these failures could let an attacker run code inside the server’s PHP process.

Researchers demonstrated remote code execution through both Apache/mod_php and application-level PHP-FPM paths for the first vulnerability, and against a real-world Apache/mod_php application for the second. 

These were problems in PHP itself, not something an administrator could fix by simply updating a WordPress plugin. It was a fundamental and nasty security hole.

How bad were the flaws?

PHP’s advisories rate both vulnerabilities 9.2, or critical, under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0. Exploitability depends on the PHP build, server configuration, extensions, and application behavior. The advisories do not establish that every PHP installation can be compromised. PHP released fixes in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12. The potential exposure is substantial: As of November 11, W3Techs reported that PHP powered 68.8% of websites whose server-side programming language it could identify. 

According to the PHP Foundation’s account, a developer investigating issues from a 2024 security audit spotted the out-of-memory problem, but no concrete attack path was established then. Proposed fixes risked compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service problems, or changes across PHP extensions.

On August 11, Calif researcher Ryan A. reported remote code execution from the same underlying problem. From that date, fixing it became the PHP Foundation security team’s top priority. OpenAI independently reported the same underlying flaw. Wiz supplied additional attack vectors on August 24, and OpenAI reported more on September 18.

How the PHP security patch came apart

In response, PHP’s maintainers coordinated fixes with researchers and distributors. Then details about the release process began leaking.

On October 20, the CVE identifiers circulated publicly, accompanied by an incorrect release time and severity score. PHP responded by issuing a warning and moving the release forward a day, to October 21 at 14:00 UTC. Calif, one of the reporting security companies, then mistakenly published a video demonstrating its proof of concept. Although the video was deleted, copies circulated. PHP also acknowledged that mitigation advice given to critical infrastructure providers might have leaked.

In short, the information environment was already a mess before Chainguard published anything.

But the PHP Foundation maintained that its remaining coordination window still served a purpose: specifically that distributors were packaging the fixes, and releasing immediately would leave many users without a straightforward update path. At 07:41 UTC on October 21, Chainguard published its patched images anyway — six hours and 19 minutes before the agreed-upon time.

The PHP Foundation criticized this move: “Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix.” That meant, it argued, that “any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release.”

A patched binary protects the person who installs it. It can also tell an attacker where to look.

That was the PHP Foundation’s central objection. A patched binary protects the person who installs it. It can also tell an attacker where to look.

Moore’s defense: The advantage had already shifted to the attackers

Moore doesn’t dispute that releasing patched binaries can help attackers. He argues that, by then, the advantage an embargo was supposed to preserve had already eroded.

While defenders alone know about a vulnerability, he told The New Stack, confidentiality gives them time to prepare. Once attackers have enough information to exploit it, withholding available fixes can reverse that advantage: attackers can act, while users outside the embargo cannot protect themselves.

“If we see exploitation in the wild, it’s incumbent upon us to release it,” Moore said. In his account, reports from other security vendors were what pushed Chainguard toward that conclusion.

Moore said Chainguard learned on the Friday before the release that PHP had a vulnerability, pointed its vulnerability-hunting harness at the software, and found the vulnerability or produced a proof of concept within hours. That is Chainguard’s account of its own research. But it helps explain the company’s thinking in breaking the embargo: If your tools can find the bug quickly, you have to consider whether attackers’ tools can too.

He also disputed the implication that Chainguard simply went off on its own. According to Moore, other embargo participants woke Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc to discuss the situation while PHP maintainers in Europe were asleep. Moore declined to identify those participants.

Moore accepted that Chainguard made the final decision. It does, however, distinguish the company’s account of a disputed emergency decision from an account in which it ignored everyone else without discussion.

The evidence supports concern, not certainty

Public evidence supports Chainguard’s concern that attackers were already targeting the flaws. For example, Amazon Threat Intelligence reported a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt against its MadPot honeypot network on October 17, four days before public disclosure. It also reported proof-of-concept exploits beginning around 02:00 UTC on October 21, followed by additional attempts from anonymized infrastructure over the next six hours. Some of that activity clearly preceded Chainguard’s 07:41 release.

Cloudflare likewise reported observing attack traffic targeting its customers before the official release. It said its free and paid web application firewall protections were enabled by default starting at 03:02 UTC on October 21.

So, no, Chainguard was not imagining hostile interest in these bugs.

But Amazon included an important qualification: “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.” The PHP security team, meanwhile, said it examined the circulating proofs of concept and “did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure.”

Those statements are not necessarily contradictory. A honeypot can record a request intended to exploit a vulnerability without establishing that it can achieve remote code execution against a real application. Likewise, PHP’s failure to find a functional public exploit does not prove that no attacker privately possessed one.

Subsequent evidence should not be confused with what was known that morning. On October 26, CISA added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. That confirms exploitation was known by then; it does not establish when the first successful compromise occurred or whether Chainguard’s early release enabled it.

Welcome to security incident response. The evidence rarely arrives neatly labeled.

Did the binaries give attackers something they lacked?

Moore’s second argument is narrower. Attackers were already probing the relevant code, so publishing patched binaries might not have helped much.

“I don’t see any evidence that what we did helped the attackers in ways that they didn’t already have,” he told TNS. He acknowledged that comparing patched and unpatched binaries can identify vulnerable code, including with AI-assisted disassembly. But identifying the code, he argued, isn’t necessarily the same as building a working exploit.

Fair enough. Locating a memory-corruption bug and reliably turning it into remote code execution are different engineering problems.

Still, this defense has limits. Evidence that some attackers knew where to look does not establish that every prospective attacker did. Nor does it establish that the patch contained no useful clues beyond the vulnerability’s location. Chainguard’s argument depends on how much actionable information was already available and how reliable it was.

The same restraint applies to the accusation against Chainguard. Publishing the binaries created an opportunity to study the changes. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that a particular compromise happened because Chainguard released early.

The two sides were assessing different risks. Chainguard emphasized the danger of withholding a ready patch from users while hostile activity was visible. PHP emphasized the danger of distributing new information before the wider ecosystem could update. Both risks were real. 

AI makes the timing problem worse

The broader concern is that AI-assisted vulnerability research could shorten the time defenders have to respond. The public reports cited here do not establish whether the pre-release PHP2Shell attempts used AI, or that this was the first incident of its kind. 

For Moore, the PHP dispute fits a larger problem: attackers’ ability to turn vulnerability information into an exploit may outrun defenders’ ability to build and distribute a fix.

He described a scenario in which a Chromium patch becomes public, and an attacker develops an exploit faster than it takes to compile the browser. That was a warning about where the industry is heading, not a claim that this exact scenario had occurred.

“You literally cannot produce builds fast enough,” he said. And the build is only the beginning. Even if Chainguard produces an updated image quickly, customers still have to incorporate it, rebuild their applications, test them, and deploy.

Faster does not mean instantaneous, and a supplier’s release time is not a customer’s remediation time.

That is the uncomfortable part of the “patch faster” answer. Faster is useful. Faster does not mean instantaneous, and a supplier’s release time is not a customer’s remediation time.

Moore’s proposed longer-term response is to reduce the number of vulnerabilities that require this race in the first place. He discussed with TNS the work toward ABI-compatible replacements for foundational software components in Rust, along with formal verification techniques intended to rule out particular classes of defects. These remain engineering ambitions to evaluate.

They also do not settle, in the eyes of Chainguard’s critics, what the company should have done on October 21. A future with fewer memory-corruption bugs would be welcome, but administrators dealing with the current bugs still need a workable disclosure process, they would argue.

The lesson is bigger than Chainguard

It would be easy to see this incident as only a story about one vendor breaking the rules. It would be equally easy to see it as a story about an agile security company rescuing users from a slow-moving upstream project. It’s not that simple.

PHP’s own postmortem acknowledges a deeper failure. The foundation calls that delay “a structural failure,” involving both decision-making and insufficient resources.

Finding bugs faster doesn’t automatically provide the engineers needed to fix them safely. And getting a patch ready at one company doesn’t mean an ecosystem of distributions, hosting providers, extensions, and applications is ready to deploy it.

Many people jumped to attack Chainguard for its call. For instance, Jay Gazlay, CISA’s acting associate director for vulnerability management, said at an October 28 Red Hat conference in Washington: “that type of behavior is dangerous, and we’ve got to be careful about holding embargoes.”

There may still be room to repair the relationship. Federal News Network, citing Politico, reported that PHP Foundation Executive Director Elizabeth Barron expressed disappointment with Chainguard but hoped to restore trust and continue collaborating.

Moore called it “a really tough call” between “two really, really bad choices.” He’s right. 

Maintainers and distributors need to agree in advance on when to lift an embargo early, who makes that decision, and how other distributors will get fixes to their users.

We need to do this as soon as possible. Otherwise, the next incident will end the same way, with vendors arguing about who broke the embargo. At the same time, administrators try to work out whether they can patch before somebody breaks their servers.

The post Chainguard defends its choice to break the PHP security embargo: “We own the decision.” appeared first on The New Stack.
Chainguard’s CTO says attackers already had a head start when it broke the PHP2Shell embargo. The evidence backs his concern, but not his certainty.
